# How to Use AI to Create a Clear Client Handoff Brief

URL: https://kristamashore.ai/articles/ai-client-handoff-brief
Pillar: The AI-Run Business
Published: 2026-08-11T13:53:25.945Z
Author: Krista Mashore

A client handoff gets easier when the next person can see what was promised, what is finished, and what happens next. This practical AI workflow helps you turn notes, messages, and files into one useful brief without asking AI to guess.

Use AI to create a client handoff brief by giving it approved project notes, asking it to sort facts into a fixed structure, and checking the result against the source material before anyone acts on it. The goal is not a polished summary for its own sake. The goal is to make the next responsibility clear. A handoff can happen when a client moves from sales to delivery, when one contractor takes over from another, or when you pause a project and return to it later. Without a shared brief, people search through inboxes, repeat questions, and make decisions from incomplete context. A short, accurate document gives the work a home. If you want the step by step version of that, read How to Use AI to Turn Meeting Notes Into a Decision Log . Start with the handoff outcome Before you open an AI tool, answer one question: what should the next person be able to do after reading this brief? That answer keeps the document practical. For example, the outcome might be: “The project manager can schedule the next client call,” or “The new copywriter can finish the approved service page.” Those are clearer than “summarize the project.” Tell AI the outcome, the reader, and the point at which responsibility changes. We go deeper on this in How to Use AI to Turn a Repeated Task Into an SOP . Do not begin with a large pile of unrelated information. Gather the material that someone needs for the next decision: The client’s stated goal and the problem being addressed The work that was agreed to What has been completed and approved What remains open Decisions already made and who made them Relevant deadlines, preferences, files, and contact details The next action, owner, and question that still needs an answer If a detail is not needed for the next step, leave it out. A handoff brief should reduce searching, not become another archive. Use a fixed brief structure AI produces a more useful draft when you give it headings. Use a structure that matches the way you run projects: Handoff purpose: Explain why responsibility is changing and what the reader needs to do. Client goal: Record the client’s goal in plain language. Use the client’s wording when it is available. Agreed scope: List what is included and identify anything that was discussed but not agreed. Status: Separate completed, in progress, waiting, and not started. Decisions: Record the decision, date if provided, and decision maker. If the date is missing, say so. Open questions: Turn gaps into questions instead of guesses. Files and links: Add only the files and links supplied for this handoff. Next action: Name one owner and one next step. Add a due date only when one is confirmed. This structure also helps you spot a weak handoff. If you cannot name the next action, the project may need a decision before it needs a new document. Give AI a careful instruction Your instruction should set boundaries. Here is a reusable starting point: “Create a client handoff brief for [reader] using only the notes below. Organize the information under these headings: Handoff purpose, Client goal, Agreed scope, Status, Decisions, Open questions, Files and links, and Next action. Do not infer missing facts. Do not create names, dates, prices, commitments, or deliverables. If information is missing or contradictory, label it for review. Separate confirmed facts from questions. Keep the language plain and concise. End with a five-line review list of details I should confirm before sharing.” Then paste the source notes below the instruction. If the material contains sensitive information, remove anything the reader does not need. You can also replace a person’s name with a role while you draft, then add the correct name during your own review. That is the same question behind How to Use AI to Build a Client Onboarding Checklist , which walks through it in detail. Ask for a source check After the first draft, ask AI to make a second pass: “Compare this brief with the source notes. List every statement that is not directly supported, every contradiction, and every open item that lacks an owner.” This turns the tool into a checking assistant rather than the final authority. Review the list yourself. AI can organize supplied material, but you remain responsible for whether the brief is accurate, appropriate, and ready to share. Review the brief in three passes A quick review catches more than a long prompt. Read the draft three different ways. Pass one: factual accuracy. Compare names, commitments, status labels, files, and dates with the original material. Delete anything that cannot be supported. If two notes conflict, preserve the conflict as an open question instead of choosing a side. Pass two: responsibility. Look at every open item. Does it have one owner? Is the next action a real action, such as “send the revised outline,” rather than a vague phrase such as “continue the project”? If an item belongs to the client, say that clearly. Pass three: reader clarity. Imagine you are seeing the project for the first time. Can you understand why the handoff is happening, what has already been approved, and what to do next? Cut background that does not help the reader act. Turn the brief into a repeatable business habit Save the approved structure as a template. Keep the headings stable so each handoff feels familiar, even when the work changes. You can pair this with a decision log for project choices and an SOP for repeated delivery tasks. Set a simple trigger: create the brief when a project changes owner, enters a new phase, pauses for more than a short period, or requires a specialist. The trigger matters more than the software. A document that exists at the right moment is more useful than a perfect document created too late. Finally, share the brief with a clear note: “Please review the open questions and confirm the next action.” That invites correction while the context is still fresh. Once the recipient confirms it, store the final version with the project files and use it as the starting point for the next update. Your next step Choose one active project and collect the notes that currently live in different places. Give AI the fixed instruction, ask it to mark gaps, and complete the three review passes before sharing anything. You will quickly see whether the problem is missing information, unclear ownership, or a process that needs a better home. When you’re ready to build this kind of workflow into the way you run your business, Learn the AI System .

## FAQ

Q: What should a client handoff brief include?
A: Include the client goal, agreed scope, completed work, open items, important context, decisions, risks, files, contacts, and the next action. Keep facts separate from questions or suggestions.

Q: Can AI create a handoff brief from meeting notes?
A: Yes, you can give AI notes and ask it to organize only the details provided. Review every section against the original notes before sharing the brief.

Q: How do I stop AI from inventing missing details?
A: Tell it not to infer, fill gaps, or create dates and names. Ask it to mark missing information as a question for review.

Q: Who should receive the handoff brief?
A: Send it to the person responsible for the next step and, when appropriate, the client. Share only the information each recipient needs for the work.

Q: How often should I create a handoff brief?
A: Create one whenever responsibility changes, a project pauses, or a client needs a clean summary before the next phase begins.

# How to Use AI to Build a Pre-Sale Answer Guide

URL: https://kristamashore.ai/articles/ai-pre-sale-answer-guide
Pillar: AI Content to Client System
Published: 2026-08-10T13:55:27.368Z
Author: Krista Mashore

If prospects keep asking the same questions before they buy, you can turn those conversations into a useful answer guide with AI. This process helps you organize your thinking, write in your voice, and give people a clearer next step.

Yes, you can use AI to build a pre-sale answer guide, but the useful material has to come from your real conversations. Start with questions prospects ask before they hire you, give AI the context for each question, and then edit every answer until it sounds like you. The finished guide can help a potential client understand your process and decide whether a conversation makes sense. This is a simple way to turn sales conversations into helpful content. You are not guessing what your audience wants to know. You are listening for the points where people pause, hesitate, compare options, or ask what happens next. There is a fuller breakdown of this in How to Use AI to Turn Client Questions Into Better Content . What a pre-sale answer guide does A pre-sale answer guide is a focused collection of answers for people who are considering your service. It is not a giant FAQ page filled with every question your business has ever received. It should address the questions that affect a buying decision. For a coach, that might include how the work begins, what a first session covers, and what someone should prepare. For a real estate agent, it could cover the first planning conversation, the information needed to discuss a move, or how the agent helps a homeowner think through options. For a consultant, it might explain what a project includes, how decisions are made, and what the client receives at the end. The guide gives your prospect a clearer picture before the next conversation. It also gives you a reusable source for emails, posts, call preparation, and follow-up. This connects directly to How to Use AI to Qualify New Business Inquiries . Collect the questions before you open AI Do not begin by asking AI to invent common questions. Begin with your own notes. Look through recent emails, call notes, direct messages, intake forms, and questions you remember hearing. You do not need to include names or private details. You only need the wording and meaning of the recurring concern. Write each question on its own line. Then add a short note answering three things: What is the person really trying to decide? What part of your process would reduce confusion? What should the person do after reading the answer? These notes matter because a question often carries a deeper concern. “How long does this take?” may really mean, “Can I fit this into my schedule?” “What do I need before we start?” may mean, “Will I be prepared, or will I feel behind?” Your guide becomes stronger when it addresses the concern underneath the words. Give AI a clear writing assignment Once you have the raw material, ask AI to organize it into a guide. Tell it who the guide is for, what service you offer, what you want the reader to understand, and what tone to use. Include your notes in the prompt instead of relying on a vague request. You can use a prompt like this: “I am creating a short pre-sale answer guide for people considering [service]. Below are real questions I hear and my rough notes. Organize them into five to ten helpful sections. For each section, write the question as a prospect might ask it, answer it in plain language, and end with one reasonable next step. Do not add claims, promises, prices, policies, or details that are not in my notes. Keep the tone warm, direct, and conversational.” The practical side of this is covered in How to Use AI to Create a Clear One-Page Offer Brief . That last instruction protects the quality of the draft. AI can make writing sound complete by filling gaps. You want it to show you where information is missing, not quietly create an answer you did not approve. Shape each answer around a decision Review the draft one question at a time. A useful answer usually has four parts: Answer the question first. Do not make the reader search through a paragraph for the point. Add the context they need. Explain the part of your process that makes the answer meaningful. Set a clear boundary. If the answer depends on the person, project, market, or situation, say so plainly. Offer one next step. Invite the reader to complete a simple action, such as reviewing your offer, sending a question, or booking a conversation. For example, an answer about your first conversation should tell the reader what the conversation is for. It should not promise a particular outcome before you know the person’s situation. An answer about your process should explain the sequence you actually follow. It should not imply that every client receives the same path when your work changes from person to person. Make the guide sound like you The first draft may be orderly but still feel generic. Read it out loud. Mark sentences you would never say in a conversation. Replace broad statements with the words you use when explaining the service to a real person. Add small details that clarify your approach, such as what you ask first, what you review, what you send after a call, or how you decide on the next step. These details do not need to be dramatic. They help a reader picture what working with you feels like. Ask AI for editing help only after you have supplied your voice. You might say, “Keep my meaning and vocabulary. Remove repetition, shorten long sentences, and flag any answer that sounds like a promise or includes a detail not supported by my notes.” Then make the final decisions yourself. Turn one guide into a small content system Do not let the completed guide sit in a folder. Use it as a source document. Ask AI to create one short post from each question, a follow-up email that answers the three most common concerns, and a list of questions to ask during your next sales conversation. You can also use the guide to improve your offer page. If several questions point to the same confusion, your page may need a clearer explanation. If a question appears repeatedly in calls, make the answer easy to find before someone contacts you. Keep a simple review habit. When a new question comes up, decide whether it belongs in the guide. If it does, add the real answer and update the related content. If it does not, keep it in your notes for later. This keeps the guide connected to actual conversations. Use the guide as a trust-building resource A good pre-sale answer guide does not pressure a reader into buying. It helps the right person understand your offer and helps the wrong-fit person recognize that sooner. That saves time for both of you. Start this week with five questions you have answered more than once. Add your rough responses, ask AI to organize them, and edit the result until every sentence is accurate and natural. Put the guide where a prospect can use it, then pay attention to which questions keep appearing. Those questions are telling you what your next helpful piece of content should answer. If you want to turn common buyer questions into a clear pre-sale guide your team can use for content and follow-up, learn the AI system .

## FAQ

Q: What should go into a pre-sale answer guide?
A: Include questions prospects ask before buying, the context behind each question, a direct answer, and one clear next step. Leave out questions that do not help someone decide whether your offer fits.

Q: Can AI write the answer guide by itself?
A: AI can help organize notes and create a first draft, but you should supply the real questions, correct the details, and approve the final wording. Your judgment makes the guide useful.

Q: How many questions should the guide include?
A: Start with five to ten questions that come up often. A short guide that answers real concerns is more useful than a long list of generic questions.

Q: Where can I use the finished guide?
A: You can use it as a website resource, a follow-up document, a sales-call preparation tool, or a source for future posts and emails. Choose the format your prospects already use.

# How to Use AI to Turn a Service Promise Into a Delivery Checklist

URL: https://kristamashore.ai/articles/ai-service-promise-delivery-checklist
Pillar: The AI-Run Business
Published: 2026-08-09T14:04:16.041Z
Author: Krista Mashore

A service promise is easy to write and easy to forget once the work begins. This practical AI workflow turns the promise into a delivery checklist your clients can understand and your business can follow.

Yes, you can use AI to turn a service promise into a delivery checklist. Give AI the promise you make, the result the client expects, and the way the work usually unfolds. Then ask it to separate your process into stages, tasks, owners, handoffs, and client decisions. You still approve the result, but you no longer have to build the first draft from a blank page. This matters because a vague promise creates a vague delivery experience. A client may hear "we will improve your marketing," while you are thinking about a review, a strategy session, three drafts, and a follow-up call. A checklist makes the invisible work visible. It also gives you a simple way to spot missing steps before they become delays. There is a fuller breakdown of this in How to Use AI to Turn a Repeated Task Into an SOP . Start with the promise, not the task list Before you open an AI chat, write one sentence that describes what the client is buying. Avoid a list of activities. Describe the change, decision, or finished item the client should have when the work is complete. For example, a consultant might start with: "I help a local business create a practical 30-day lead follow-up plan." A real estate agent might write: "I help a seller prepare a clear plan for presenting and promoting a home." A coach might write: "I help a business owner leave each session with a focused next-step plan." These sentences are starting points, not claims about a guaranteed result. Next, add five kinds of context: The client and the situation they bring. The beginning and end of the engagement. The major stages between those points. What you need from the client at each stage. What is outside the service boundary. That last item is easy to skip. If you don't state what isn't included, AI may quietly add work that sounds reasonable but doesn't belong in your offer. A good checklist protects your time as much as it supports the client. Use AI to map the work in five passes 1. Ask for a plain-language process map Paste your service promise and context into AI and ask for a process map written for a person who has never seen the work before. Ask for five to seven stages at most. Each stage should have a name, a purpose, and a clear finish line. This connects directly to How to Use AI to Create a Clear One-Page Offer Brief . Use a prompt like this: "Here is my service promise and the way I currently deliver it. Organize the work into clear stages. For each stage, list the purpose, the task I complete, the information I need from the client, and the sign that the stage is complete. Do not add services I did not describe. Mark any assumption as a question." The instruction to mark assumptions is useful. It prevents a polished guess from being mistaken for your actual process. Read the draft and answer every question before you keep going. 2. Turn stages into observable tasks Ask AI to break each stage into tasks that someone could recognize as done or not done. "Review strategy" is too broad. "Review the current offer, identify the primary audience, and record three unanswered questions" is easier to check. Keep the list short enough to use. If a task contains several verbs, ask whether it should become two tasks. If a task has no visible finish, add an output such as a note, draft, decision, appointment, or approval. Outputs help you keep momentum when the work is busy. The practical side of this is covered in How to Use AI to Build a Client Onboarding Checklist . 3. Add ownership and handoffs Have AI add an owner to every task: you, the client, a team member, or a shared responsibility. Then ask it to flag every point where work changes hands. Handoffs cause many avoidable delays. The client may need to approve a draft. You may need access to a document. A team member may need to prepare an asset before you can review it. Put those moments directly into the checklist, including the information that must be present before the next person starts. 4. Create internal and client-facing versions Your internal checklist can include private notes, quality checks, time estimates, and reminders about risk. Your client-facing checklist should answer four questions: What happens next? What do you need from me? What will I receive? How will we know this stage is complete? Ask AI to create the client version using calm, plain language. Remove internal shorthand. Replace phrases like "waiting on asset" with "Please send the approved logo before the content draft can be finalized." The client doesn't need every detail of your work. They do need a reliable view of their part in it. 5. Test the checklist with exceptions A process that only works in the perfect case isn't ready. Give AI three common exceptions: the client responds late, the client changes direction, or required information is missing. Ask it to show where the checklist should pause, what decision is needed, and how the next step should be recorded. Don't ask AI to invent a policy for sensitive matters. Use it to expose gaps in the process, then decide your own response. Your judgment belongs in the final checklist. Make the checklist easy to run Organize the finished version in the same place where the work happens. Use one row or card per task. Include the task name, owner, status, due point, required input, and finished output. If the service has optional paths, label them clearly instead of mixing them into the main flow. Use language that describes action. "Send the draft for review" is stronger than "Draft review." Add a definition of done to tasks that often create confusion. For a content review, that might mean the client has either approved the draft or listed specific changes in one place. At the end of an engagement, ask AI to compare the checklist with your notes. Which steps repeated? Which step created a question? Where did you do work that the original promise didn't mention? Update the process only after you decide whether the change belongs in the service, in your boundary, or in a separate offer. Your next step Choose one service you deliver often and write its promise in one sentence. Collect the steps you already follow, even if they live in scattered notes. Ask AI to map the stages, mark assumptions, and create internal and client-facing checklists. Review every line, test one real engagement, and revise what made the work clearer. AI is most useful here as a thinking partner and organizing assistant. You bring the promise, the standards, and the judgment. The checklist gives those decisions a form you can repeat. If you want a larger system for turning your expertise into repeatable business workflows, learn the AI system .

## FAQ

Q: What should I give AI before asking for a delivery checklist?
A: Give it your service promise, the client outcome, the stages of the work, your boundaries, and the decisions the client must make. Specific input produces a more useful first draft.

Q: Can AI create the final process for my business?
A: AI can organize and question your process, but you should review the draft. You decide what your business actually promises, who owns each task, and what requires professional judgment.

Q: How detailed should a client-facing checklist be?
A: Show the stages, client responsibilities, expected handoffs, and next step. Keep private notes, internal estimates, and sensitive information in your internal version.

Q: What if my service changes for every client?
A: Create a repeatable core checklist with optional branches. The core protects consistency, while the branches let you adapt without rebuilding the whole process each time.

Q: Where should I keep the finished checklist?
A: Put it where you already manage client work, such as your project workspace or shared document system. The best location is one you and your team will actually check.

# How to Use AI to Build a Better Pre-Call Question Sheet

URL: https://kristamashore.ai/articles/ai-pre-call-question-sheet
Pillar: The AI-Run Business
Published: 2026-08-08T14:08:03.327Z
Author: Krista Mashore

A good pre-call question sheet helps a client arrive with useful context instead of making you spend the first part of the conversation collecting basics. Here’s a practical way to use AI to draft one, review it, and make it sound like you.

Use AI to draft a short, specific pre-call question sheet from your offer, your audience, and the purpose of the conversation. Then edit every question until it sounds like something you would actually ask. AI should help you think through the structure, not replace your judgment. A pre-call sheet is useful when a conversation could go in several directions. It gives the other person a chance to gather details, and it gives you a clearer starting point. That matters whether you are preparing for a coaching consultation, a real estate conversation, a lending call, or a project discussion. Start with the decision the call needs to support Before you ask AI for questions, write one sentence that describes the purpose of the call. For example: “I need to understand whether this person is ready for a three-month coaching engagement.” Or: “I need enough context to decide whether this property conversation is a fit for my services.” If you want the step by step version of that, read How to Use AI to Qualify New Business Inquiries . That sentence keeps the form from becoming a general biography. You are not trying to learn everything about a person. You are gathering the context needed for a useful conversation and a clear next step. Give AI these five pieces of context: What you offer and who it is for. What the call is meant to clarify. What information you need before making a recommendation. What information you do not need or should not request. The tone you want the person to feel when they complete the sheet. Do not paste private information that the person has not agreed to share. You can describe the type of client and the type of call without including identifying details. A prompt that gives AI enough direction A vague request such as “Write a client questionnaire” usually creates a list that could belong to any business. Give AI a role, a goal, and limits. Try this: Prompt: “Act as a thoughtful intake designer for my business. I help [audience] with [specific problem]. This pre-call sheet is for a [type of call], and the decision we need to support is [decision]. Draft 10 questions that help me understand the current situation, desired outcome, obstacles, timing, and fit. Use plain language. Avoid questions that feel invasive, repetitive, or like a sales trap. Mark the five questions that are essential if the person only has a few minutes.” That first draft is not the finished sheet. Read it and mark three categories: questions you want to keep, questions that need a rewrite, and questions that reveal something you do not actually need to know. Shape the questions around five useful areas 1. Current situation Begin with what is happening now. Ask the person to describe the situation in their own words. “What are you trying to solve right now?” is often more useful than asking them to choose from a long list of problems. A short answer can give you language to revisit during the call. We go deeper on this in How to Use AI to Prepare for a Difficult Client Conversation . 2. Desired outcome Ask what a meaningful improvement would look like. Keep the question concrete: “What would you like to be different after we work together?” This helps separate a broad wish from an outcome you can discuss responsibly. 3. Obstacles and past attempts Ask what has made the problem difficult and what they have already tried. This prevents you from repeating advice that did not fit. It also helps you understand whether the person wants information, a plan, accountability, or a different kind of support. 4. Timing and readiness Timing questions can be simple. Ask whether there is a date, event, deadline, or reason the conversation matters now. You can also ask what needs to be true before they take the next step. Do not pressure someone to provide an answer they do not have. 5. Call expectations End by asking what they want to leave the call with. They may want a recommendation, a few options, a rough plan, or a candid assessment of fit. Knowing that beforehand makes it easier to guide the conversation. Make the sheet easier to complete Once AI has grouped the questions, ask it to reduce repetition and place the questions in a natural order. Then make the sheet practical for a real person. Put the most useful questions first. Use one idea per question. Explain why a detailed answer helps when that is not obvious. Offer a “not sure yet” option when it makes sense. Keep optional questions separate from required ones. Ask for short answers unless a longer answer is genuinely helpful. Next, ask AI to create two versions: a five-question quick version and a longer version for people who want to share more. You can choose the right version based on the call type without rebuilding the process each time. Run a tone and usefulness review AI-generated forms can sound formal even when the underlying questions are good. Paste the draft back into AI with a sample of your own writing and ask for a tone review. Tell it to point out phrases that sound stiff, vague, judgmental, or overly promotional. You can ask for alternatives, but you should choose the final wording. Then do a human test. Read each question aloud. If you would never say it in a conversation, rewrite it. If two questions would produce the same answer, keep the clearer one. If a question makes you wonder what you would do with the answer, remove it or explain its purpose. Turn responses into a call plan The real value of the sheet comes after it is completed. Ask AI to organize the responses into a one-page preparation note with four sections: The person’s stated situation and desired outcome. Questions or details that need clarification. Topics to discuss during the call. A few possible next steps, clearly labeled as options rather than promises. Review that note yourself before the call. Correct anything AI misunderstood. Separate what the person actually said from your interpretation. This keeps the conversation grounded and makes it easier to listen instead of trying to construct the entire call in real time. After the call, you can use the same structure to record the agreed next action, the person’s open questions, and the date for follow-up. That creates a clean handoff from preparation to follow-through. For a related process, see how to turn a discovery call transcript into next actions . Keep improving the question sheet Do not change the sheet after every single call. Review it after several conversations and look for patterns. Which questions produce answers you use? Which ones are skipped? Where do people seem confused? Ask AI to summarize those patterns from anonymized notes, then decide what to change. Your question sheet should become shorter and clearer over time. It should help the right person arrive prepared, help you ask better follow-up questions, and help both of you agree on what happens next. That is a small workflow, but it can remove a surprising amount of scattered preparation from your week. If you want to build the larger system around content, follow-up, and business operations, learn the AI System .

## FAQ

Q: What should a pre-call question sheet include?
A: It should ask about the person's current situation, desired outcome, obstacles, timing, and what they want from the conversation. Keep questions connected to the decision they are trying to make.

Q: Can AI write the questions without knowing my business?
A: AI can draft a starting point, but the quality depends on the context you provide. Give it your offer, audience, call goal, boundaries, and examples of questions you already ask.

Q: How many questions should I send before a call?
A: Use only the number you can review before the conversation. A short set of focused questions is usually more useful than a long form that feels like homework.

Q: Should every prospect receive the same question sheet?
A: Start with a core set, then adjust a few questions for the offer, audience, or kind of conversation. The sheet should feel relevant while still giving you consistent information.

Q: How do I keep AI-generated questions from sounding generic?
A: Add real language from your calls, remove questions you would not ask out loud, and ask AI to rewrite the sheet in your natural tone. Read the final version as if you were the person filling it out.

# How to Use AI to Write a Personal Referral Request

URL: https://kristamashore.ai/articles/ai-personal-referral-request
Pillar: AI Content to Client System
Published: 2026-08-07T13:53:56.265Z
Author: Krista Mashore

A referral request works best when it feels personal, specific, and easy to answer. Here is a simple AI workflow for drafting one without handing over your relationships or your voice.

Yes, you can use AI to write a personal referral request, but you shouldn't ask it to invent the relationship. Give it the real context, the kind of person you help, and the specific introduction you would appreciate. Then edit the draft until it sounds like you. That distinction matters. A referral request is not a broadcast promotion. It's a small conversation with someone who already knows you, has seen some of your work, or has chosen to stay connected. AI can help you find the words, but the trust comes from the truth behind them. Before you decide, it helps to read Past-Client AI Nurture: The 12-Month Touch System That Brings Referrals Back . A simple AI workflow for a better referral request Start with one person, not a list. Open a note and write five plain-language answers: Who is this person to me? What do I appreciate about our relationship? What problem do I help solve? What kind of person might benefit from that help? What would a useful introduction look like? Don't polish your answers. The rough version is useful because it contains details a generic prompt won't. You might write that the person attended a workshop, introduced you to a colleague last year, or often talks with business owners who feel stuck with follow-up. Keep the information accurate and share only what the draft needs. Then ask AI to draft a message with a clear role. You could say: Prompt: “Act as an editing partner. Write a short referral request to someone I already know. Use the context below. Make it warm, specific, and easy to answer. Do not exaggerate, pressure the reader, or add facts I didn't provide. Include one natural question and keep the message conversational. Here is the context: [paste your five answers].” The request for an editing partner helps set the tone. You're asking for a draft, not handing over the relationship. Give the message a useful shape A good referral request usually has four parts. The parts don't need to appear as formal sections in the final message, but they give you something to check. 1. Reconnect with a real detail Begin with the reason you're reaching out. Mention a conversation, project, event, or shared interest that actually exists. “I was thinking about our conversation on client follow-up” is stronger than “I hope you're doing well” by itself. If you want the step by step version of that, read How to Use AI to Build a 30-Day Prospect Follow-Up Plan . This detail does two jobs. It reminds the reader who you are in relation to each other, and it shows that the message wasn't copied to everyone in your contacts. If AI gives you a vague opening, replace it. 2. State the problem you solve Describe the problem in the words your audience might use. A coach might help a business owner turn scattered ideas into a repeatable content plan. A lender might help a buyer understand the next steps in a financing process. A consultant might help a team document work that currently lives in one person's head. Keep this part narrow. “I help businesses grow” gives the reader nothing useful to remember. A clear problem gives them a way to recognize a possible referral. 3. Describe the referral you want Ask for a situation, not a perfect lead profile. You can say, “If someone in your circle mentions that they have plenty of ideas but no consistent way to turn them into content, would you feel comfortable introducing us?” We go deeper on this in Email Nurture Sequences That Don't Sound Like AI: The Three-Pass Method . That request gives the person a listening cue. They don't have to search their entire network or guess what you mean by “anyone who needs help.” They only need to remember a conversation that fits. 4. Make the next step small One simple question is enough. You might ask whether anyone comes to mind, or whether the person would be comfortable forwarding a short introduction. Don't attach a long explanation to the first request. If they respond, you can provide the details they need. Use AI to improve the draft, not to make it sound bigger After AI gives you a first draft, run three editing passes. Truth pass: Check every claim, name, date, and relationship detail. Delete anything that wasn't in your notes. Voice pass: Read the message aloud. Replace words you don't normally use. Shorten sentences that feel formal or polished in the wrong way. Friction pass: Ask whether the reader knows what you're asking, why you're asking them, and what they should do next. If any answer is unclear, revise the message. You can ask AI to help with each pass. Try: “Point out any sentence that sounds generic, pressuring, or unsupported. Do not rewrite yet.” Then make the decisions yourself. A useful review should reveal weak spots without turning your message into a different person's voice. You can also ask for three versions with different levels of familiarity: one for a close contact, one for a past client, and one for a professional acquaintance. Use the version that matches the relationship. A past client may welcome a direct request, while a newer contact may need a little more context first. What to leave out of an AI referral workflow Don't paste an entire contact record into a writing prompt just because you can. A referral request rarely needs a person's private history, personal circumstances, or unrelated notes. Use the minimum context needed to draft a respectful message. Don't ask AI to create urgency you don't feel. A message that implies a deadline, scarcity, or special opportunity can damage a relationship when none of those things are real. Ask clearly, give the other person room to decline, and keep the tone steady. Don't send the same request to every person in your network. You can reuse the structure, but the opening, problem, and request should fit the individual. Personalization isn't adding a first name to a template. It's showing why this person is a sensible person to ask. Turn one request into a repeatable habit If you want referrals to become part of your normal business rhythm, create a small record after each conversation. Note who you contacted, why the relationship made sense, what you asked for, and whether you need to follow up. AI can turn those notes into a simple reminder list or help you draft a respectful follow-up later. Keep the follow-up connected to the original request. You might say, “I wanted to follow up on my note from last week. No pressure at all. I was curious whether anyone came to mind who is trying to solve that problem.” If the person says no, thank them and leave the relationship in good shape. You can also use the same workflow after delivering a useful result, completing a project, or reconnecting with a past client. The timing should make sense in the relationship. A request is easier to receive when it follows a real conversation rather than appearing without context. Your next step Choose one person who already knows your work. Write the five rough answers, ask AI for a short draft, and edit it in your own voice. Before you send it, make sure the request names one problem, one kind of introduction, and one easy next step. That is enough to begin. You don't need a complicated campaign. You need a truthful message, a clear reason for reaching out, and the discipline to treat the response as a conversation instead of a transaction. If you want a larger system for turning AI into consistent content, follow-up, and business support, learn the AI System .

## FAQ

Q: Can AI write a referral request for me?
A: Yes. AI can help organize your context and draft a message, but you should review every sentence before sending it. The final request should reflect your real relationship and a genuine reason to reach out.

Q: What information should I give AI first?
A: Give it the relationship, the person's likely need, the help you provide, the kind of introduction you would value, and the tone you want. Leave out private information that isn't needed.

Q: How long should a referral request be?
A: Keep the first message short enough to read quickly. A few clear paragraphs are usually enough to reconnect, explain who you can help, and make one simple request.

Q: Should I send the AI draft exactly as written?
A: No. Treat the draft as a starting point. Replace generic wording, add a real detail from your relationship, and remove anything that doesn't sound like something you would say.

Q: What if I don't know exactly who to ask for?
A: Ask for a situation instead of a job title. For example, you might describe the kind of problem someone is facing and invite the person to think of anyone who has mentioned it recently.

# How to Use AI to Turn a Workshop Into a Content Brief

URL: https://kristamashore.ai/articles/ai-workshop-content-brief
Pillar: AI Content to Client System
Published: 2026-08-06T14:24:28.915Z
Author: Krista Mashore

A workshop can contain weeks of useful ideas, but only if you give those ideas a structure before you start writing. This practical workflow shows you how to use AI to sort the material into a focused content brief, check the message, and choose the next pieces to create.

Yes, you can use AI to turn a workshop into a content brief, but the useful result comes from giving the tool a clear job. Ask it to identify the audience's problem, organize the strongest teaching points, separate examples from claims, and recommend a small set of content pieces. Then you review the brief before anything is published. This matters because a workshop usually has more material than one article can hold. If you ask AI to simply summarize the recording, you may get a long recap with no clear message. A content brief gives the material a destination. It helps you decide what to say, who needs to hear it, and what the reader should do next. Start with the business outcome Before you paste in notes or a transcript, write one sentence that explains why you want to reuse the workshop. Keep it specific. For example: I want to help independent agents understand how to answer common seller questions, then invite them to request a planning conversation. The sentence does two jobs. It tells AI what to look for, and it gives you a test for every recommendation. If a proposed topic does not support the audience or the conversation you want to start, it probably does not belong in this brief. Choose one primary audience as well. Small business owners is broad. A solo consultant who has useful expertise but posts inconsistently gives the writing a real person to serve. You can create another brief for another audience later. Give AI clean source material Use the best material you already have: a transcript, workshop outline, speaker notes, chat questions, or your own follow-up notes. You do not need to make the source perfect first. You do need to label each item so the tool can tell the difference between what you taught, what an attendee asked, and what you want to add later. This connects directly to Email Nurture Sequences That Don't Sound Like AI: The Three-Pass Method . Remove information that should not appear in public content. That may include private contact details, confidential business information, or a participant's personal situation. A brief can be accurate without repeating sensitive details. If you have a transcript, ask AI to preserve the meaning while cleaning filler words and repeated points. If you only have an outline, tell it that the source is incomplete. That small instruction helps you spot places where a draft needs your judgment rather than invented detail. A useful first prompt You can begin with a prompt like this: You are helping me plan content for [audience]. The business goal is [goal]. Review the workshop material below. First, list the audience's main problem in one sentence. Then group the teaching into three to five themes. For each theme, show the practical lesson, the supporting example from the source, and any statement that needs my review. Do not add facts that are not in the source. End with three possible content angles. That prompt asks for sorting and judgment support. It does not ask AI to make up a story, add a statistic, or present an unverified promise. Shape the raw material into a brief Once AI has grouped the workshop, ask it to format the result into a brief with these sections: Audience: Who is this for, and what are they trying to solve? Working title: A clear question or promise, not a vague topic. Core message: The one idea the reader should remember. Three to five teaching points: The smallest useful sequence for understanding the idea. Source examples: Examples from the workshop that make the teaching concrete. Review notes: Claims, numbers, names, or recommendations you must check. Call to action: The next reasonable step for this audience. Content formats: The primary piece and two or three smaller follow-ups. The core message is the most important section. If you cannot say it in one or two sentences, the workshop may contain several separate articles. Split them. One focused article is easier to write, easier to read, and easier for a potential client to remember. Choose one primary piece Do not begin by asking for ten social posts. Choose the piece that deserves the deepest thought. That might be an article answering the audience's main question, an email that teaches one decision, or a short guide that helps someone take the next step. Then ask AI to create a simple outline for that piece from the approved brief. Give it boundaries such as the intended reader, approximate length, required sections, and tone. Tell it which examples are approved and which points still need review. After the primary piece is finished, reuse its approved ideas for shorter content. This is where a workshop becomes a system rather than a one-time writing task. One lesson can become a useful article, a short email, several conversation prompts, and a follow-up question for your audience. For a related approach, see AI content repurposing from one video . The same principle applies here: approve the central message before adapting it into smaller formats. Use human review where it counts AI is helpful at sorting, labeling, and suggesting structure. You remain responsible for the meaning. Read the brief and ask four questions: Does this describe a problem my audience actually recognizes? Would I say the core message this plainly in a real conversation? Are the examples faithful to the workshop? Does the next step fit the reader's level of interest? Pay close attention to confident wording. A draft can make an ordinary suggestion sound like a guarantee. Replace promises with clear guidance. If a point depends on a current rule, product detail, price, statistic, or outside claim, mark it for verification or leave it out. Your own language also matters. Add the phrases you use with clients, the questions people ask before they buy, and the distinctions you make that others skip. Those details are what turn a generic summary into content with a point of view. Turn the brief into a repeatable weekly habit At the end of each workshop, save four things in one folder: the source material, the cleaned transcript or notes, the approved brief, and the final content. The next time you teach the topic, you can update the brief instead of starting from a blank page. You can also maintain a short list of audience questions that the workshop did not answer. Feed those questions into your next planning session. The article How to turn client questions into better content can help you build that list from real conversations. Keep the workflow simple: collect, sort, review, create, and reuse. The goal is not to produce the largest number of posts. The goal is to make your best teaching easier for the right person to find and act on. What a strong brief gives you A strong brief gives you a clean starting point, a clear audience, and a message that can survive across formats. It also shows you where your source material is thin. That is valuable. You can return to the workshop, add your own example, or remove a point that is not ready to publish. When your workshop has a clear offer behind it, connect the content to that offer without forcing the sale. A focused offer document can help you make that connection; see how to create a clear one-page offer brief with AI . Start with your next workshop or training. Give AI the audience, the business goal, and the source material. Ask for themes, examples, review notes, and a few content angles. Then make the final call yourself. That is how you turn teaching you have already done into content that keeps working for your business.

## FAQ

Q: What should I give AI before asking for a content brief?
A: Give it the workshop transcript, outline, notes, or a combination of those materials. Also include the audience, the business goal, and any points that must remain accurate.

Q: Can AI create the whole content plan from one workshop?
A: It can suggest a plan, but you should choose the final topics. Review the suggestions for accuracy, audience fit, and whether each piece supports a real business conversation.

Q: How long should a content brief be?
A: Keep it short enough to use. A few focused sections covering the audience, promise, key points, proof, call to action, and formats are usually enough for a first draft.

Q: How do I keep the content from sounding generic?
A: Give AI examples of your real language, specific audience questions, and clear points of view. Then edit the draft so it sounds like a person with an opinion, not a summary tool.

Q: What should I do after the brief is approved?
A: Create one primary piece first, such as an article or email. Use the approved message to guide shorter posts, a follow-up email, or a conversation prompt.

# How to Use AI to Create a Clear One-Page Offer Brief

URL: https://kristamashore.ai/articles/ai-one-page-offer-brief
Pillar: The Authority Agent Operating System™
Published: 2026-08-05T13:52:37.495Z
Author: Krista Mashore

A one-page offer brief gives you a clear reference point for sales conversations, content, and follow-up. Here is a practical way to use AI to build one from what you already know about your business.

Use AI to create a one-page offer brief by giving it your real business notes, asking it to organize the offer into a fixed set of sections, and then editing every claim until the page sounds like you. The goal is not to have AI invent a clever slogan. The goal is to make your offer easier to explain, sell, and turn into useful content. If your offer lives in scattered notes, old sales emails, voice memos, and your own head, every conversation starts from scratch. A short brief gives you a dependable reference point. It can guide a discovery call, a landing page, a follow-up email, or a post that answers a question your audience is already asking. Before you decide, it helps to read The Authority Agent Operating System: The 5 Layers Every Service Business Needs in 2026 . What belongs in a one-page offer brief? Keep the document practical. A reader should understand the offer without needing a long background story. Start with these sections: Best-fit person: Describe who the offer is for and what situation they are in now. Problem: State the costly, frustrating, or time-consuming problem the person wants to address. Desired outcome: Describe the change your service is designed to help create. Keep the wording specific without promising a result you cannot control. Method: Summarize the main steps, conversations, deliverables, or decisions included in the work. Boundaries: Say what the offer does not include. Clear boundaries prevent the page from becoming a list of everything you could possibly do. Proof: Add only evidence you are permitted to use, such as your own relevant experience, a process explanation, or an approved example. Next step: Tell the right person what to do next, such as booking a call, completing an application, or sending a question. This structure works for a coach, consultant, real estate agent, lender, or creator because it connects the offer to a real business conversation. It also gives AI enough shape to help without handing over your judgment. Gather source material before you prompt AI can arrange information, but it cannot know the details of your service unless you provide them. Collect the material you already have. You might include your current website copy, a service description, a list of deliverables, questions prospects ask, notes from recent calls, and a short explanation of who should not buy the offer. If you want the step by step version of that, read Brand Voice Fingerprinting: How to Capture How You Write So Claude Sounds Like You . Do not paste private information that the brief does not need. Remove names, contact details, financial records, and anything confidential. A useful source packet can be general and still be concrete. For example, instead of sharing a client identity, write, “The buyer had many inquiries but no consistent follow-up process.” Also separate facts from hopes. “I send a weekly review and provide three planning calls” is a description of your process. “Every client doubles revenue” is a result claim that would need support. Leave unsupported claims out. We go deeper on this in How to Use AI to Turn Notes Into a Client-Ready Proposal . Use a prompt that asks for structure Ask AI to act as an editor and organizer, not as the owner of your business. You can start with a prompt like this: “Create a one-page offer brief from the source material below. Use these headings: Best-fit person, problem, desired outcome, method, boundaries, proof, and next step. Keep the language plain and specific. Do not invent facts, results, testimonials, credentials, or features. Mark any missing information with [NEEDS MY INPUT]. Give me a draft and then a short list of claims I should verify.” Paste your source material below the prompt. If you use Claude, you can place the approved source material and writing preferences in a Project, then ask for a fresh draft when the offer changes. The important part is the instruction: AI should work from your material and identify gaps instead of filling them with guesses. Edit the draft in three passes The first draft is a sorting exercise. Your editing is what makes the brief useful. Check accuracy. Read each sentence and ask whether it describes what you actually do. Remove invented details, broad promises, and language that makes the service sound larger than it is. Check clarity. Replace abstract words with observable actions. “Improve your business” is vague. “Create a weekly follow-up routine for new inquiries” gives the reader something they can picture. Check fit. Read the page as one specific person. Would they recognize their current problem? Would they understand whether the offer is for them? Would the next step feel clear? Read the page out loud. If you would never say a sentence in a real conversation, rewrite it. Your brief should sound like a strong explanation you could give on a call, not like a brochure assembled from general business language. Turn one brief into daily business assets Once the brief is approved, keep it as a source document. Ask AI to create related assets while preserving the same audience, promise, boundaries, and next step. You can request a discovery-call opening, five educational posts, a short FAQ email, a follow-up message, or a page of objections and responses. Review each asset against the brief. This prevents a common problem: your website says one thing, your sales conversation says another, and your follow-up introduces a third version of the offer. Consistent language makes it easier for a potential client to understand what you do and decide whether to continue. You can also feed recurring questions back into the brief. If people repeatedly ask whether the service includes a certain task, add that answer to the boundaries or method section. If prospects use a phrase that describes the problem better than your original wording, consider adding their plain-language phrase to the document. Keep the brief alive, but keep it short A one-page brief is not meant to become your entire operations manual. It is a decision tool. It should help you answer four questions quickly: Who is this for? What problem does it address? How do I help? What should the right person do next? Store the approved version where you can find it, and name it clearly. When you change the offer, update the brief before asking AI to create new sales or content materials. That small habit gives every new draft a better starting point. AI is most useful here when it reduces the friction between what you know and what you need to communicate. You supply the experience, boundaries, and judgment. AI helps you sort the material into a clear working document. That is enough to make your next conversation, email, and piece of content more focused. If you want a broader system for turning your expertise into repeatable business workflows, learn the AI System .

## FAQ

Q: What is an AI offer brief?
A: It is a short working document that explains who your offer serves, the problem it addresses, the outcome you provide, what the process includes, and what a qualified person should do next. AI helps organize your raw material, but you approve the final message.

Q: What should I give AI before asking it to write the brief?
A: Give it your current offer description, notes from real conversations, common questions, deliverables, boundaries, and any proof you are allowed to share. Specific source material produces a more useful first draft.

Q: Should my offer brief include pricing?
A: Only if pricing is already part of your public sales process. If the price depends on scope, leave it out and explain how someone can ask for the right next step.

Q: Can I use one offer brief for every audience?
A: Use one core brief as your source of truth, then create audience-specific versions when the problem, language, or buying context changes. Keep the underlying promise consistent.

Q: How often should I revise the brief?
A: Review it when your offer changes or when repeated conversations reveal confusion. You do not need to rewrite it on a schedule if the message still matches the work you deliver.

# How to Use AI to Build a 30-Day Prospect Follow-Up Plan

URL: https://kristamashore.ai/articles/ai-30-day-prospect-follow-up-plan
Pillar: AI Content to Client System
Published: 2026-08-04T14:07:12.410Z
Author: Krista Mashore

A good follow-up plan should help a prospect make a decision, not pressure them into one. Here is a simple way to use AI to organize the conversation, find useful next steps, and create a month of personal follow-up.

Yes, you can use AI to build a 30-day prospect follow-up plan from one conversation. The useful version starts with your actual notes, separates what the prospect said from what you assume, and turns their questions into a small sequence of helpful messages. You still review and send each message yourself. The goal is not to fill a calendar with reminders. The goal is to remember the person's situation well enough to follow up with something relevant. There is a fuller breakdown of this in How to Use AI to Qualify New Business Inquiries . Start with the conversation, not a generic template Before you ask AI to write anything, gather the notes you already have. These might come from a discovery call, a voice memo after a meeting, an email exchange, or a few handwritten points. You do not need polished notes. You need the raw material. Pull out five things: The result the prospect wants. The problem or frustration they described. The questions they asked. The concern that may slow down a decision. The next step, timing, or permission you discussed. Be careful with the difference between a fact and an interpretation. “They said they need to review the budget” is a fact from your conversation. “They are probably worried about price” is an interpretation. Ask AI to label those separately so your follow-up does not treat a guess as something the prospect told you. Use one clear prompt to create the plan Give AI a job, a source, and boundaries. You could start with a prompt like this: “Act as my follow-up planning assistant. Use the conversation notes below to create a 30-day nurture plan for one prospect. Separate confirmed details from assumptions. Suggest five or fewer touches. For each touch, include the purpose, a useful topic, the best format, and a short draft. Do not invent facts, promises, deadlines, testimonials, or resources. Keep the language warm, direct, and low-pressure. Every touch must connect to something the prospect said or asked.” This connects directly to Email Nurture Sequences That Don't Sound Like AI: The Three-Pass Method . Then paste your notes. If the notes include sensitive information, remove anything AI does not need to complete the task. The more specific your source material is, the less likely the drafts are to sound like messages copied from a marketing sequence. Ask for a plan before you ask for finished copy. This gives you a chance to reject a weak idea early. If AI suggests three versions of “just checking in,” the problem is not the wording. The problem is that the follow-up has no purpose. Give every touch a reason to exist A practical 30-day plan might include a small number of moments such as these: After the conversation: Send a concise recap of what you heard, the agreed next step, and one question if something remains unclear. When you can answer a question: Share a short explanation, example, checklist, or process that helps with the issue the prospect raised. When a concern needs room: Acknowledge the concern without trying to talk the person out of it. Invite them to tell you what information would help. Near the timing you discussed: Refer back to the timing in your notes and ask whether the situation has changed. At the end of the period: Offer a clear next step, or make it easy for the prospect to say that now is not the right time. These are categories, not a rule that every prospect needs five messages. Some people need two thoughtful follow-ups. Others need more time and a useful resource between conversations. The plan should reflect the relationship and the prospect's stated pace. Turn the plan into messages that sound like you AI often produces language that is tidy but lifeless. Your notes can fix that if you add a short voice guide. Tell AI whether you write in short paragraphs, whether you prefer a conversational opening, which words you never use, and how direct your calls to action should be. The practical side of this is covered in How to Use AI to Turn Client Questions Into Better Content . You can also paste a few examples of your own writing and ask for a draft that follows those patterns without copying any sentence. Then edit the draft with three questions: Would I say this out loud to the person? Does this message prove that I remember their situation? Is there a useful reason to respond, even if they are not ready to buy? Delete flattery that you do not mean. Delete urgency you cannot support. Delete broad claims about what everyone needs. A personal follow-up is often shorter after editing. Build a review step into the workflow Do not let the plan disappear into a document. Put each touch into the place where you manage follow-up, then add a review step before sending. Your review can be as simple as checking four fields: source note, intended date, purpose, and draft. Before a message goes out, confirm that the timing still makes sense. Check names, numbers, links, and any details about your service. Make sure the message does not promise an outcome you cannot promise. If the prospect has already answered the question, do not send a message that repeats it. This human check is also where you decide whether the right next action is a message, a call, a useful introduction, or no contact for a while. AI can help you see the options. It should not decide what respect looks like in your relationship. Measure the quality of the conversation You do not need a complicated report. After each touch, record what happened in plain language. Did the prospect reply? Did they ask a better question? Did they clarify their timing? Did they say no? A clear no is useful information too, because it keeps you from treating silence as a permanent invitation. At the end of 30 days, ask AI to summarize the thread and suggest one of three actions: continue with a specific reason, schedule a future check-in the prospect agreed to, or close the loop respectfully. Include the original notes and your follow-up record so the suggestion is grounded in the actual exchange. You can reuse the same workflow for a coach reviewing an enrollment conversation, a consultant waiting on a proposal decision, a lender helping a borrower understand next steps, or an agent staying connected with a future client. The structure stays consistent. The source conversation and the useful answer change. The simple standard for better follow-up A good AI-assisted follow-up plan should help you remember, respond, and make the next step clear. It should not make you sound busier, louder, or more automated. Start with one conversation this week. Ask AI to identify what the person actually needs, draft a short plan, and point out every assumption. Then revise the plan until each touch earns its place. When the workflow is built around listening, AI gives you more consistency without taking the relationship out of your hands. If you want a larger system for turning your knowledge and follow-up into a repeatable business process, learn the AI System .

## FAQ

Q: What should I give AI before asking for a follow-up plan?
A: Give it your notes from the conversation, the prospect's stated goal, concerns, timing, and the next step you discussed. Remove private details that are not needed for the writing task.

Q: How often should I contact a prospect during 30 days?
A: Choose a rhythm you can maintain and that fits the conversation. A few useful, spaced-out touches are usually better than sending a message every day.

Q: Should AI send the follow-up messages automatically?
A: Keep a human review step. AI can organize ideas and draft language, but you should check the timing, facts, tone, and whether each message gives the prospect a real reason to hear from you.

Q: What if I do not have enough information for 30 days of content?
A: Do not fill the calendar with generic messages. Ask AI to create fewer touches, suggest one useful resource, and identify the question you should answer next.

# How to Use AI to Turn Meeting Notes Into a Decision Log

URL: https://kristamashore.ai/articles/ai-meeting-notes-decision-log
Pillar: The AI-Run Business
Published: 2026-08-03T14:03:14.597Z
Author: Krista Mashore

Meeting notes are only useful when they help you remember what was decided and what happens next. This practical AI workflow turns rough notes into a decision log your business can actually use.

Use AI to turn meeting notes into a decision log by giving it the raw notes, asking it to separate decisions from discussion, and requiring it to label every action with an owner, deadline, and next check-in. Then review the result yourself before it becomes the official record. This matters because a meeting can feel productive while still leaving everyone with a different understanding of what happens next. A decision log gives you one place to see what was chosen, why it was chosen, who is responsible, and what still needs an answer. What a useful decision log contains A decision log is not a transcript. It is a short operating record. Each entry should help someone understand the decision without rereading an hour of conversation. The practical side of this is covered in How to Use AI for a Weekly Business Review . Date and topic: Identify when the discussion happened and what business issue it covered. Decision: State the choice in one clear sentence. Reason: Capture the main factors that led to the choice. Owner: Name the person responsible for the next action. Due date: Include a specific date when one exists. Open questions: List anything that could change the decision. Next review: Record when the team will check progress or revisit the choice. That structure keeps the record useful for a solo business owner as well as a small team. You are creating a memory for the business, not just a summary for the people who attended. The five-step AI workflow 1. Gather the real notes Start with the notes you actually have. They may come from a notebook, a voice memo, a meeting transcript, or a rough document with incomplete sentences. Do not spend an hour rewriting them first. The roughness is exactly what the workflow is meant to handle. Before sharing them, remove information that should not be entered into your chosen AI tool. That can include passwords, payment details, private health information, or sensitive personal information. If a detail is not needed to understand the decision, leave it out. 2. Give AI the business context AI produces a better working draft when it knows the purpose of the meeting. Tell it what kind of business you run, what outcome the meeting was meant to produce, and who the audience for the final log will be. Before you decide, it helps to read How to Use AI to Turn a Repeated Task Into an SOP . For example, you might write: “I run a consulting business. These are rough notes from a planning meeting about a new service. Create a decision log for me and my assistant. Keep decisions separate from ideas, and do not assume a detail that is not in the notes.” That last instruction is essential. It tells the tool to organize the information without pretending that missing information is settled. 3. Ask for separation, not a polished summary A broad request such as “summarize this meeting” may produce a readable paragraph, but it can blur the difference between a suggestion and a final choice. Ask for distinct sections instead. Use a prompt like this: “Review the notes below. Return four sections: decisions made, action items, unresolved questions, and ideas that were discussed but not approved. For every action item, include the owner and deadline only when stated. If the notes are unclear, write ‘needs confirmation.’ Do not invent names, dates, reasons, or commitments.” This format gives you a first pass that is easy to inspect. It also creates a useful boundary around what AI is allowed to infer. In a business record, a visible gap is safer than a confident guess. If you want the step by step version of that, read How to Use AI to Turn a Messy Inbox Into a Daily Action List . 4. Turn the draft into a repeatable record Once the sections look accurate, ask AI to place them into a consistent template. Keep the template simple enough that you will use it every time. Ask for columns or headings such as decision, reason, owner, due date, status, and next review. If your business has several types of meetings, create a slightly different version for sales, operations, content, or client work. The basic fields can stay the same while the questions change. For a client meeting, you might add “client preference” and “client approval needed.” For a content meeting, you might add “audience problem” and “publication channel.” The record should reflect the work, not force every conversation into an identical shape. 5. Review and assign the next move Read the draft against the original notes. Check names, dates, decisions, and wording that could be interpreted more than one way. Correct anything that is wrong or too certain. Then choose one next move. Save the approved log where you keep business records, send a short follow-up message, or add the action items to your task system. AI has helped prepare the record, but the system becomes valuable only when a human uses it to move work ahead. How to keep the log accurate The most common problem is allowing a polished output to feel more reliable than the source notes. Set a few rules that protect the record. Ask AI to mark uncertain information instead of filling it in. Keep decisions and proposals in separate sections. Use exact dates when a deadline was stated. Do not assign an owner unless the meeting notes support that assignment. Have the decision maker approve the final wording when the choice affects a client, contract, budget, or team responsibility. You can also ask AI to run a quality check after it creates the log: “List every statement in this decision log that is not directly supported by the notes.” Review that list before you share the document. It gives you a second way to catch accidental assumptions. When this workflow is most useful Use it after meetings where choices get buried inside conversation. That may include deciding which offer to promote, setting a content theme, reviewing a lead process, planning a client project, or assigning work for the week. It is especially helpful when you are the person carrying most of the business in your head. A written record reduces the need to remember every detail and makes it easier to return to the reasoning behind a choice. It can also show you which decisions keep reopening because a question, owner, or deadline was never recorded. This workflow is not a substitute for judgment. It is a way to make your judgment easier to see and easier to act on. Start with one recurring meeting, use the same prompt for a few weeks, and adjust the template when you notice a missing field. Make meeting memory part of your operating system Your business does not need more notes. It needs notes that lead somewhere. When every important meeting produces a short decision log, you can review the past, see current commitments, and prepare the next conversation without starting from zero. That is a small AI workflow, but it solves a real business problem: good conversations disappearing before the work is finished. Build the habit around one meeting this week, then connect the approved actions to the rest of your follow-up process. Learn the AI System to build practical workflows that help your business create, follow up, and keep moving with fewer manual steps.

## FAQ

Q: What should I give AI before asking it to organize meeting notes?
A: Give it the raw notes, the meeting purpose, the names or roles of people involved, and any known deadlines. Remove confidential details that do not belong in the tool you are using.

Q: Can AI decide what my business should do?
A: AI can sort, summarize, compare, and surface open questions. You should make the decision and review the final record before sharing it.

Q: How often should I update a decision log?
A: Update it after each meaningful meeting or decision. A short, consistent update is more useful than waiting until several weeks of notes have piled up.

Q: What if the meeting notes are incomplete?
A: Ask AI to mark uncertain details and create a list of questions to confirm. Do not let it fill gaps with guesses.
