# Claude Skills: Build Your Brand Voice Skill Once and Reuse Forever

URL: https://kristamashore.ai/articles/claude-skills-brand-voice-skill
Pillar: Claude for Dummies: The AI Tools That Actually Matter
Published: 2026-05-24T16:06:09.351Z
Author: Krista Mashore

Anthropic introduced Claude Skills in 2025 and they're the missing layer most business owners don't know exists. Here's how to build your brand voice Skill first.

You finally got Claude sounding like you in one chat. The cadence was right, the words were yours, you stopped flinching when you read the output back. And then you opened a new conversation the next day and Claude was back to writing like a LinkedIn coach with a thesaurus. I know the feeling. The fix is a Claude Skill, and once you build one for your brand voice, that one specific problem becomes solved forever across every conversation, every Project, every team member you bring in. Skills are the thing nobody is talking about loud enough yet, and they should be. Let me walk you through what they are, and then how to build the single most valuable one for your business: your voice. What a Claude Skill actually is Anthropic introduced Skills in 2025 as a way to package up reusable instructions, examples, and reference files that Claude can load on demand inside a conversation. Think of it as a kind of recipe folder. You write the recipe once. You name it. Then when you (or your team) need that specific output, Claude knows to pull that recipe in and follow it. There is a fuller breakdown of this in Claude Projects: Setting Up Your First One (Step by Step for Business Owners) . The mechanics: a Skill is a folder with a description file (usually a SKILL.md or skill.md) that tells Claude when and how to apply it, plus any supporting files you want it to reference. Claude reads the description, decides whether the Skill is relevant, and loads it into context when it is. You don't have to remember to invoke it. The platform does the matching for you. This is a different thing from a Project. A Project is a workspace with persistent files and instructions for a specific scope of work (your business, a particular client, a particular product line). A Skill is portable. You can use the same Skill across multiple Projects, share it with teammates, or upgrade it once and have every workflow that depends on it improve automatically. Voice rules belong in a Skill. Knowledge documents belong in a Project. Both layers matter. The exact way you create and manage Skills depends on whether you're using Claude.ai, Claude Desktop, or Claude Code, and Anthropic has been shipping updates to this regularly. So I'll keep the steps tool-agnostic and you can apply them in whichever surface you use. Why brand voice is the first Skill to build Most business owners try to build their first Skill around a workflow, like an email sequence generator or a sales page outliner. That's a mistake. Workflow Skills are useful, but they'll only ever be as good as the voice they output in. If the voice is generic, the workflow Skill produces generic copy 50 times faster. That's worse than slow generic copy. That's scale on a broken foundation. This connects directly to Brand Voice Fingerprinting: How to Capture How You Write So Claude Sounds Like You . Voice is the foundation. Build it first. Once you have a voice Skill that genuinely sounds like you, every subsequent Skill (your email Skill, your social Skill, your podcast outline Skill) inherits the voice automatically and you stop fighting your AI on the same problem 200 times. Step 1: Extract your voice You can't write a voice Skill from memory. You have to extract it from actual writing you've done that you're proud of. Here's the process I use, which usually takes me about 2 hours one afternoon. Pull together 8 to 12 pieces of your own writing. Emails, social posts, sales pages, podcast intros, anything where the voice was unmistakably you and the response from your audience was strong. Paste them into a single document. Now open a Claude conversation and ask Claude to act as a voice analyst. Prompt it with something close to this: "Below are 10 samples of my writing. Analyze them and extract a voice profile. I want: sentence rhythm patterns, recurring words I actually use, words I appear to deliberately avoid, formatting tendencies, common rhetorical moves, and 3 to 5 example sentences that capture the voice at its strongest. Be specific. Don't give me adjectives." The practical side of this is covered in The 7 AI Tools Running Krista's Content Engine Right Now . Claude will give you back a draft voice profile. Read it. Some of it will be accurate, some will be off. Edit it. The edited version becomes the heart of your Skill. Step 2: Structure the Skill A good voice Skill has roughly six sections: A short description at the top that tells Claude when to apply it. Something like "Apply this Skill any time you are writing copy, social posts, emails, or any content that goes out to my audience." This is the part Claude reads to decide whether to load the Skill. A "voice in one paragraph" summary so a new collaborator (or a new Claude conversation) can get oriented fast. A "use these words" list. Specific words you actually use. Not adjectives like "warm" but the literal words like "agents," "lenders," "systems," "stack." A "never use these words" list. The banned terms. For me that's the entire corporate vocabulary plus the AI tells: use, use, dive, dig in, work through, path, open up, solid. Put yours in writing. A "patterns to avoid" section. The triplet pattern, the question-then-list-answer pattern, the suspiciously perfect transition, the "it's not X, it's Y" formulation. If you don't put these in writing, Claude will drift back to them every time. A "examples" section with 4 to 8 short passages of your actual writing. These are the highest signal part of the Skill. Claude pattern-matches against examples more strongly than against rules. Save it. Name it something obvious like "krista-voice" or "[yourname]-voice." Make sure the description field is clear enough that Claude will know when to trigger it. Step 3: Test it (this is where most people stop too soon) Spin up a fresh conversation. Don't give Claude any other context, just trigger the Skill or upload it depending on your tool. Then ask Claude to write a piece of content you'd normally write yourself. Read the output out loud. Yes really. Out loud. If it sounds like you ranting in your kitchen, congrats. If it sounds like a thoughtful corporate cousin of you, the Skill isn't done yet. Common gaps I see on first drafts: not enough banned words listed (the AI tells slip back in), examples that are too short to anchor rhythm, rules that contradict each other so Claude picks the safer/blander rule. Go fix the Skill, test again. Three rounds and you'll have something that holds. Pattern interrupt: my first voice Skill took me four attempts before it sounded right. The fourth attempt was different because I stopped trying to describe my voice and just dumped in 6 full paragraphs of stuff I'd actually written. The examples did most the work. So if you're stuck, add more examples. A real example of the difference Same prompt, "Write a 150-word LinkedIn post about why most agents fail at consistent content." Without the voice Skill, Claude wrote something starting with "In today's competitive real estate landscape, content consistency separates thriving agents from those struggling to grow." That sentence alone has three of my banned phrases. With the voice Skill loaded, Claude wrote, "Most agents don't fail at content. They fail at the 90 seconds before the content, which is the part where they decide what they actually think. Then they sit in front of a phone with nothing to say and call it writer's block." That second one I'd actually post. The first one I'd delete. That gap is the gap a voice Skill closes. If you want the full voice extraction template I use with my coaching clients, plus the rest of the AI authority system that sits around it, that's all inside Level Up . I built it specifically for coaches and consultants who need their AI to sound like them, not like everyone else's AI.

## FAQ

Q: Where do I actually create a Skill?
A: The exact creation flow depends on the Claude surface you use (Claude.ai, Claude Desktop, Claude Code, or the API). Anthropic's documentation has the current step-by-step. Check there because the UI has shifted a couple of times since launch.

Q: Are Skills available on the free plan?
A: Skills availability has varied by plan since launch. Verify current plan inclusions on Anthropic's pricing page before assuming. If you're a business owner you want a paid plan anyway.

Q: Can I share a Skill with my team?
A: Yes, on team-level plans. Sharing across personal accounts has been more limited. Check current sharing options if this is critical to your setup.

Q: Can a Skill override a Project's instructions?
A: Skills and Project instructions work together. The Project sets persistent context, the Skill adds specialized behavior on demand. They don't usually conflict if you've written both cleanly. If they do, the Skill's specificity tends to win in the moments it's active.

Q: How long should a voice Skill be?
A: Most of mine are between 1,500 and 3,000 words including examples. Long enough to be specific, short enough that Claude can actually hold it. The examples eat most of the word count and that's correct.

Q: What's the next Skill to build after voice?
A: Whatever output you create most often. For most coaches and consultants that's either an email Skill or a long-form content Skill. Build the one that saves you the most weekly hours first.

# Brand Voice Fingerprinting: How to Capture How You Write So Claude Sounds Like You

URL: https://kristamashore.ai/articles/brand-voice-fingerprinting-claude
Pillar: The Authority Agent Operating System™
Published: 2026-05-24T16:06:09.351Z
Author: Krista Mashore

A 5-step process to extract your writing voice into a reusable Claude Skill or Project. Stop sounding like a LinkedIn carousel had a baby with a corporate apology.

You read your own AI-written email out loud yesterday, didn't you. And about three sentences in you cringed because it didn't sound like you, it sounded like a LinkedIn carousel had a baby with a corporate apology letter. Don't worry. You're in the right place. The reason almost every AI output sounds like that is not because the AI is broken. It's because nobody has bothered to capture how you write. Not adjectives. Not vibes. The patterns, sentence shapes, word choices, and weird little habits that make your writing recognizable. This process has a name and I call it brand voice fingerprinting. It's the single highest-impact thing you can do with AI right now, and most people skip it. There is a fuller breakdown of this in Claude Skills: Build Your Brand Voice Skill Once and Reuse Forever . Here's how I do it. Plus how I package it into a reusable Claude Skill that I can drop into any project. What "voice fingerprinting" means A fingerprint is a unique pattern. Yours is different from mine. Same with how you write. You probably: start more sentences with "And" or "So" than most people avoid certain words on purpose (mine: that corporate L-word that means "use" makes me twitch) have a few signature phrases you've been using for years without noticing have a sentence-length pattern (mine is short, then long, then medium) show up differently in emails than in social posts contradict yourself on purpose sometimes use parentheses for personality, not only clarification Voice fingerprinting is the process of cataloguing all of that and turning it into instructions an AI can follow. Then packaging those instructions so you don't have to retype them into every new chat. Step 1: Pull your raw material Open a folder somewhere. Could be Google Drive, could be Notion, could be a single Word doc. Now collect at least 30 samples of your actual writing. I said 30. Not three. Mix it up. Pull from: The last 10 emails you wrote to clients (skip the boilerplate ones) Five social posts you wrote yourself (not the ones a VA wrote) Three sales pages or long-form pieces Five voice memos transcribed into text (this one's underrated, the way you talk leaks into how you should write) Five short replies you sent in DMs or Slack Anything else that feels like "yeah, that's me" The reason you need this much material is that AI is a pattern-matching machine. Patterns need data. Three samples isn't a pattern, it's a coincidence. This connects directly to The Authority Agent Operating System: The 5 Layers Every Service Business Needs in 2026 . Step 2: Run the extraction prompt This is where the magic happens, and it's a long prompt, so plan for it. Open Claude. (You can do this in ChatGPT too. The output is roughly the same. I prefer Claude for this particular task because in my testing it's been better at picking up on stylistic quirks instead of summarizing tone, but your mileage may vary.) Paste all 30 samples in. Then ask: Analyze these writing samples and produce a voice fingerprint document. Include: signature words and phrases this person uses repeatedly. Words they appear to avoid. Average sentence length and rhythm patterns. How they open and close pieces. The kinds of openings they use (questions, declarative statements, observations). Their use of contractions, fragments, parentheticals. Their humor style if any. Their go-to analogies. Their relationship with their reader (formal, friend, mentor, peer). Any forbidden patterns (em-dashes, triplet sentences, etc.) the writing seems to avoid. You'll get back a document that's probably 1,000-2,000 words. Read it. Mark the parts that feel right. Cross out the parts that don't. Add anything important the AI missed. This is now your draft voice fingerprint. Step 3: Turn it into a Skill Here's where Claude Skills come in. Anthropic released Skills in 2025 as a way to package reusable capabilities for Claude. A Skill is, in plain terms, a folder with a SKILL.md file plus any supporting docs. You drop it into Claude and it knows when to use it based on the description you give. The practical side of this is covered in Claude Projects: Setting Up Your First One (Step by Step for Business Owners) . For brand voice, I structure the Skill folder like this: SKILL.md (the main instructions, including the description that tells Claude when to use it) voice-fingerprint.md (the document you produced in step 2) writing-samples.md (a handful of your best raw samples, included so Claude can pattern-match against them) do-not-use.md (a list of forbidden words and patterns) The SKILL.md description is the most important part. It's the thing Claude reads to decide whether to load the skill at all. Mine says something like "Use this skill anytime you're writing in Krista Mashore's voice, including blog posts, emails, social posts, ads, and anything else customer-facing." Boring on purpose. Specific. If you're not technical, a Claude Project with custom instructions can do roughly a lot of what a Skill does, and it's a lot easier to set up. The trade-off is that Skills are portable across projects and chats. Projects are siloed. Step 4: Test it on three specific outputs Don't trust your fingerprint until you've stress-tested it. Run it on three things you write often: A nurture email to your list A LinkedIn or Instagram post A reply to an inbound DM or sales question For each, generate three drafts using your voice skill or project. Read each out loud. (Yes, out loud. Your ear catches things your eye misses.) If it sounds like you, great. If it sounds like an AI doing an impression of you, the fingerprint needs work. I have a coaching client, we'll call him James. He's a fitness coach. His first fingerprint pass said he uses "lots of metaphors and a friendly, encouraging tone." That description could fit half of Instagram. Useless. The second pass said he opens most emails with a one-sentence story from his week, uses food metaphors specifically (not generic ones), and ends with a question he expects the reader to answer in their head. That's a fingerprint. The difference between draft one and draft two is the difference between AI that's almost-you and AI that sounds like you walked into the room. Step 5: Update it forever A voice fingerprint isn't a one-time project. Every few weeks, when you catch the AI saying something that's not quite right, you go update the SKILL.md or the Project instructions. I update mine maybe twice a month. Tiny tweaks. A new "don't use this word" gets added. A new pattern I've started using gets documented. (Right now I'm trying to use the word "okay" less and the phrase "so." more. We'll see if it sticks.) The MCP angle, since you asked. If you have your Claude set up with the Model Context Protocol connected to your Google Drive or Notion, you can keep your voice fingerprint living in one of those places and Claude can pull from it dynamically. Not required. Helpful for teams who need to share the same voice across multiple people. What changes when this is right Your editing time drops. A lot. I went from spending 30 minutes editing a 700-word email to about 6. That's a 24-minute swing per piece. Multiply that by the number of pieces you write a week and that's a real, recoverable block of time. Your content also gets more consistent across channels, which is what builds the kind of trust that turns followers into clients. The kind of authority that compounds. If you want the full walkthrough on how I built my own voice Skill, including the actual SKILL.md template and the extraction prompts I use, that's all inside my Level Up training. It's the same voice system I use to produce more content per week than most coaching businesses produce in a month. Grab it at kristamashore.com/LevelUp .

## FAQ

Q: Do I need a Claude Skill, or is a Project enough?
A: For most solo entrepreneurs, a Project is enough to start. Add a Skill when you want the same voice to work across multiple Projects or when you want to share it with team members.

Q: How many writing samples do I need?
A: Thirty minimum. Sixty is better. Three is a coincidence, thirty is a pattern.

Q: What if my voice has changed over the years?
A: Use samples from the last 12-18 months only. Older samples will confuse the pattern. You can fingerprint different eras of your voice if you want, but most people don't need to.

Q: Does this work for video and audio scripts too?
A: Yes, and it works better than for written content because spoken patterns are usually more distinctive. Feed in transcripts of you talking, not polished scripts.

Q: How do I know if my fingerprint is too vague?
A: If the document could describe more than one person you follow, it's too vague. A real fingerprint should feel uncomfortably specific to you, almost like reading your diary.

Q: Can I drop a few examples into Claude and skip the fingerprint?
A: You can, and it'll work okay for a single piece. But you'll be feeding the same examples into every new chat forever. A fingerprint plus a Skill or Project means you set it up once and reuse it everywhere.

# AI Document Review for Loan Files in 2026: Ocrolus, Blend, and What Lenders Should Actually Use

URL: https://kristamashore.ai/articles/ai-document-review-loan-files-2026
Pillar: Community Market Leaders®: AI for Real Estate & Lenders
Published: 2026-05-24T16:06:09.351Z
Author: Krista Mashore

Ocrolus, Blend, Maxwell, Floify. What each one actually does, who they're for, the honest tradeoffs, and where AI is allowed to make decisions in a loan file.

You're a loan officer in Phoenix. You took an application Tuesday. Borrower sent over 47 pages of bank statements, two W-2s, three pay stubs, a tax return with eight K-1 attachments, and a gift letter that has the wrong donor name on it. Your processor is on PTO. Your underwriter is buried. And you've got a 21-day close to hit because the listing agent is already nervous. You've heard the names. Ocrolus. Blend. Maxwell. Floify. Some of these your shop already pays for. Some your competitors are using. You're not entirely sure which one does what, where the AI is allowed to make decisions, and what's just marketing. Below is the honest read. This connects directly to MCP Servers Explained: The 5 to Set Up First (For Non-Technical Business Owners) . What "AI document review" actually means in a loan file Before we get to the tools, get the categories straight, because the marketing blurs them on purpose. There are roughly four jobs AI is doing in mortgage right now: Document classification and extraction. AI reads the PDF, figures out it's a bank statement, pulls the routing number, account number, transactions, and balances. This is mostly OCR plus a model. Mature, reliable, table stakes. Income calc and analysis. AI looks at pay stubs, W-2s, tax returns, business returns, and outputs a calculated qualifying income. This is harder. There's a lot of judgment in self-employed income and the AI is making real calls. Red flag and fraud detection. Inconsistencies across documents, possible alterations, suspicious deposits, identity flags. Useful as a screen, not as a final answer. Decisioning and underwriting. Whether the loan gets approved. This is where compliance gets serious and most tools deliberately stop short. Where the AI is allowed to make a call versus where it has to flag for a human is the line that matters. The good vendors are clear about this. The shaky ones are not. The four tools, honest read I'll go in the order most loan officers ask me about them. Ocrolus What it does: document classification, data extraction, and income analysis on bank statements, pay stubs, W-2s, tax returns, and some business documents. Strong on cash-flow analysis for bank statements, which is why non-QM and self-employed-heavy shops love it. It feeds processed data into your LOS or POS. Who it's for: lenders doing meaningful non-QM, bank statement loans, or self-employed volume. Also retail shops that want the data extraction layer to stop eating processor hours. The honest tradeoff: it's a data and analysis layer, not a borrower-facing experience. You still need a POS for the front end. It's a back-of-house tool. Pricing is per-document and adds up if you're not watching it. Verify current pricing and capabilities directly with Ocrolus before you sign. The practical side of this is covered in The AI-Run Business Stack Krista Uses Today (Full 2026 Breakdown) . Where AI is allowed to decide: it gives you calculated income figures and flags. A human underwriter still owns the credit decision. Treat the calc as a starting point, not the answer. Blend What it does: a homeownership platform. Mostly known as the borrower-facing POS, with extensions into close, fund, and consumer banking. AI work inside Blend is increasingly about pulling borrower data automatically (asset and income verification through pipes like FormFree, Plaid, or Finicity, depending on integrations), surfacing exceptions, and reducing the document upload back-and-forth. Who it's for: mid-to-large lenders who want a unified borrower experience and have the IT bench to integrate it. Smaller IMBs sometimes find it heavy. The honest tradeoff: it's a platform, not a point tool. Implementation is not a weekend. The upside is a much cleaner borrower experience and better data flowing into your LOS. The downside is the cost and the fact that you're consolidating a lot of vendor risk into one platform. Before you decide, it helps to read Claude vs. ChatGPT for a Non-Technical Business Owner in 2026 . Where AI is allowed to decide: mostly in routing and surfacing. Decisioning stays with your engine and your underwriters. Maxwell What it does: loan fulfillment and processing software, with AI-assisted document review, conditions, and workflow. Aimed at community lenders, credit unions, and smaller IMBs that need more processing capacity without building it themselves. Who it's for: lenders doing 50 to 500 units a month who don't have a 40-person ops team. Maxwell has historically been good at the "make a processor 30 to about half more productive" pitch. The honest tradeoff: it's narrower than Blend and less data-extraction-heavy than Ocrolus. If your bottleneck is processing capacity, this is the kind of tool that earns its keep. If your bottleneck is income analysis on complex files, Ocrolus or a dedicated income tool is closer to the target. Where AI is allowed to decide: condition clearing assistance, document categorization, status surfacing. Underwriting decisions stay with humans. Floify What it does: a POS focused on document collection, status visibility, and loan officer / borrower communication. Lighter than Blend, faster to stand up, popular with brokers and smaller mortgage banks. Who it's for: brokers, small to mid IMBs, and originator teams that want a clean POS without an enterprise implementation. The honest tradeoff: not as feature-deep as Blend on the back end. Strong on the front end and on borrower experience for the price. AI features are evolving and you should verify the current state directly with Floify before assuming parity with the larger platforms. Where AI is allowed to decide: mostly status, nudges, and document checks. Decisioning is not the play here. What about Zest AI Worth a quick mention because loan officers ask. Zest AI is on the underwriting and credit decisioning side, building models that lenders use to approve loans, primarily known in consumer and auto and increasingly in mortgage. If you're a loan officer, you're not buying Zest. Your credit shop or your investor relationships might be. It's relevant context for understanding where AI in mortgage is heading: real decisioning models, with fair-lending review baked in. Verify current mortgage applicability before assuming. Time-to-close impact, realistically Vendors love quoting "some faster closes" and similar marketing claims. The honest read from lenders I've talked with: Document extraction tools like Ocrolus can pull 2 to 5 days out of a file when the income picture is complex. Less on a clean salaried W-2 file. A real POS like Blend or Floify can compress the document-collection phase from 7 to 10 days down to 2 to 4. That's where most of the visible time savings come from. Maxwell-style processing capacity typically shows up as more files per processor per month rather than a per-file time drop. I'd push back on any vendor quoting a single "X days faster" number without telling you the file mix. Verify their numbers against your own pipeline before you sign. Compliance: the part nobody markets hard enough This is the part that determines whether AI in your loan file is a productivity gain or a regulatory problem. Things to ask every vendor before you sign: Is the AI making the decision or flagging for a human? Document the answer. How is the model audited for fair-lending impact (disparate impact analysis, model risk management documentation)? What's the data retention policy? Where does borrower PII live? Who has access? If a borrower asks for an adverse-action explanation, can your team explain the AI's role? Does the vendor's documentation satisfy your regulator (CFPB, prudential regulator, state agency) under their current AI guidance? Federal regulators and state agencies have been steadily tightening AI-in-lending expectations. Don't assume a vendor's "we're compliant" line. Get the documentation. Get your compliance officer in the room before the demo. This is the single most important thing in this whole article. Where AI is allowed to decide vs. flag for a human Simple rule of thumb that holds up well: Allowed to decide on its own: document classification, OCR extraction, status updates, missing-document detection, borrower nudges, internal task routing. Allowed to draft, human reviews: income calculations, asset verifications, exception flags, condition clearing recommendations, fraud screens. Human decides, AI only assists: anything that touches the credit decision. Adverse action. Pricing. Anything a borrower could appeal or that a regulator could examine. If a vendor sells you the third category as "fully automated," walk. How to actually pick Three questions in order: What's your real bottleneck? Document collection (POS problem, look at Blend or Floify), income analysis (Ocrolus), or processor capacity (Maxwell)? Pick the tool that solves your actual constraint, not the shiniest demo. What's your file mix? Heavy self-employed, non-QM, or bank statement = Ocrolus or a dedicated income tool. Clean salaried agency = a good POS is usually enough. What's your compliance posture? If your CO is conservative, start narrower. POS plus document extraction. Add decisioning layers later. Want the AI playbook for lenders? I work with loan officers and lending teams on the AI workflow side: how to actually use these tools day-to-day without breaking compliance, and how to position yourself with agents so you're the lender they think of first. The Level Up program covers it.

## FAQ

Q: Will AI replace loan officers in 2026?
A: No. AI is replacing parts of processing, document review, and status communication. The loan officer's job (relationship, structuring the deal, advising the borrower, working with the agent) stays very human. LOs who get faster with AI win share from the ones who don't.

Q: Can I use a consumer AI like ChatGPT or Claude on borrower documents?
A: Not without serious compliance review. Borrower documents have PII. Putting them into a general-purpose consumer AI without a business agreement and proper data handling is a problem. Stick with mortgage-specific tools that have signed the right agreements.

Q: What's the cheapest place to start?
A: A good POS that's already in your shop, used properly. Most lenders aren't using their existing tools to even a lot of their capacity. Maximize what you have before you buy something new.

Q: How do I evaluate vendor claims about time-to-close?
A: Ask for case studies with your file mix. Ask for the methodology. Ask to talk to a current customer who looks like your shop. If they can't produce all three, the number is marketing.

Q: What about Zest AI specifically for mortgage?
A: Verify directly with Zest where they sit in mortgage in 2026 and what investor relationships they have. The space is moving and what was true 18 months ago may not be true now.

Q: Should I worry about fair-lending issues with AI underwriting?
A: Yes. This is the single biggest regulatory risk in AI lending. Any decisioning model has to be tested for disparate impact and documented. If a vendor can't show you that work, walk.

# AI Content Repurposing: How to Turn One Video into Eight Social Posts, an Email, and a Blog Article

URL: https://kristamashore.ai/articles/ai-content-repurposing-one-video-eight-posts
Pillar: AI Content to Client System
Published: 2026-05-24T16:06:09.351Z
Author: Krista Mashore

One video. Ten pieces of content. The workflow took me about four months to dial in and I'm walking you through every step so you can copy it.

Pop this open if you've ever recorded a great video and watched it die after one post. That used to be me. I'd film something I was proud of, post it once, and then... silence. The video sat in a folder. The ideas inside it never reached anyone again. That's the problem this article fixes. I'm going to walk you through the exact workflow I use to turn one 22-minute video into eight social posts, one email, and a blog article. Ten pieces of content from one piece of work. I built it over about four months and it now runs in under two hours of focused time. Some of that is hands-on. Most of it is AI doing the grunt work while I supervise. Quick admission before we start. You'll see I name specific tools below. I am not loyal to any of them. If a better tool shows up next month, I'll swap it in. The workflow is the durable thing. The tools are just the muscles. The practical side of this is covered in The Authority Agent Operating System: The 5 Layers Every Service Business Needs in 2026 . The starting point: one recorded video Everything begins with a real video. Not a script. Not a teleprompter performance. A real conversation, training, or solo recording where you said something useful for 15 to 30 minutes. Mine usually clock in around 20 to 25 minutes because that's how long I can talk before I need water. Why does the length matter? Because anything shorter and you don't have enough raw material to slice. Anything longer and you'll get tired of editing before the workflow finishes. Record in 1080p minimum. Frame yourself in the upper two thirds. Leave clean space around your head so the vertical crops don't chop your face. That part is so dumb-simple but I cannot tell you how many agents send me content with their forehead cut off. Step 1: Run the video through Opus Clip Upload the full video to Opus Clip. As of mid-2026, the platform takes your long video and auto-generates short vertical clips with captions, suggested hooks, and a "virality score" for each one. I don't trust the score. I trust my eye. Before you decide, it helps to read Brand Voice Fingerprinting: How to Capture How You Write So Claude Sounds Like You . What I'm looking for in the auto-clips: A clip where I made a single, complete point A clip with a real emotion in my face (irritation, excitement, a laugh) A clip with a number or specific example in it I pick five to seven clips from each Opus Clip pass. The platform usually generates 15 to 25, so I'm rejecting more than I'm keeping. That ratio matters. If you publish all 15, you train the algorithm to think your content is forgettable. Time spent: 12 to 18 minutes. Step 2: Polish the clips inside Descript Each kept clip goes into Descript next. Why two tools? Because Opus Clip is fast at slicing, and Descript is great at fine edits. Inside Descript I: Tighten the captions (Opus Clip is mostly accurate but it gets names wrong a lot) Remove a stray "um" or a thirty-second tangent if the clip needs it Add a hard-stop at the end so the video doesn't bleed into a weird half-thought Bump the audio so the voice sits forward Descript's transcript-based editing means I delete a word and the audio cuts with it. It still feels like magic to me even though I've used it for two years now. This is also where I sometimes use Descript's Studio Sound to clean up background noise, especially if the original was filmed in a hotel room or on the road. The feature was solid the last time I used it but they iterate on it constantly, so check the current version when you set up your account. If you want the step by step version of that, read The AI-Run Business Stack Krista Uses Today (Full 2026 Breakdown) . Step 3: Caption rewrite for each platform Now the eight social posts. The clip is the same. The caption is not. I open Claude and paste in the clip's transcript along with a quick brand-voice context block. I have a saved prompt that says something like: "Here's a transcript of a short video. Write me one Instagram caption, one LinkedIn post, one TikTok caption, and one YouTube Shorts description. Each one has to sound like Krista Mashore. Direct. Confident. No corporate filler. Use my voice rules." Claude gives me four drafts. I rewrite at least two of them by hand because the AI versions always feel a hair too clean. That's the part most people skip and it's why their content sounds like every other coach. Here's a trick. If I'm tired and the AI version is close, I read it out loud. If I stumble or feel embarrassed saying any sentence, I cut it. Real speech doesn't make you cringe. Step 4: Build the email from the same source Now the email. I take the original 22-minute transcript and feed it back to Claude with a different prompt: "Pull out the single strongest teaching moment from this transcript and write me a 250-word email about it. Open with a hook for one person. End with a soft CTA to the full video." The email is shorter than what most people send. That's intentional. People skim emails on phones at red lights. 250 words is the right size. What does AI do here? The structure, the framing, the smooth flow. What do I do? I add the personal detail at the top. Something like... "I almost didn't record this video because my dog was barking the entire morning and I was over it." That kind of line doesn't come from a prompt. It comes from your actual day. Step 5: The blog article This is the heaviest piece and the one most coaches skip. They think nobody reads anymore. They're wrong. I give Claude the full transcript plus the email I just wrote plus three or four bullets of structure I want the article to follow. Claude drafts a 1,200-word blog. Then I rip into it. The rewrite usually takes me 30 to 40 minutes. I: Add specific stories from the actual recording Cut any sentence that could have been written by anybody Insert two or three "human moments" where I admit something or shift mid-thought Adjust the headers so they're real, not generic The result is an article that pulls organic search traffic for months. One video. Months of return. Step 6: The optional HeyGen layer If I want to repurpose for a different audience (Spanish-speaking, a co-marketing partner, a private community), I send a script version through HeyGen and have an avatar version generated. I use this maybe once a month. It's not a daily move for me. But when you need it, it's there. What AI does vs. what you do (the honest breakdown) AI handles: the slicing, the transcription, the first-draft writing, the structure, the captions, the audio cleanup. You handle: the original recording, the clip selection, the personality injections, the final pass before publishing, the strategic decisions about which platform gets what. If you flip that and let AI handle the personality? Your content will read like the 4,000 other AI posts in someone's feed. The whole point of the workflow is to scale your voice. Not replace it. Want me to walk you through this live? If you want to see this workflow run in real time, with the exact prompts and the screen recordings of every tool, I teach it inside Level Up. We sit down together and I show you my prompt library, the saved Claude project, and the Descript shortcuts that save me hours every week. Come join us at Level Up and I'll show you how the whole engine runs.

## FAQ

Q: Do I need every tool you mention to make this work?
A: No. The minimum stack is one clipping tool (Opus Clip or similar), one editor with transcript editing (Descript works well), and Claude for written adaptations. The rest are nice-to-haves once you've got the rhythm.

Q: How long does the full workflow take?
A: After three or four rounds, I get a 22-minute video repurposed in about 90 minutes of focused work. Your first try will take a half day. That's normal. Push through.

Q: Won't the social posts feel repetitive if they all come from one video?
A: They would if you didn't rewrite them. The clips are different moments. The captions need to be written for the platform, not pasted across all of them. AI handles a lot of that. You handle the punch.

Q: What about voiceover clips or avatars... where does HeyGen fit?
A: HeyGen comes in when you want to make extra versions in another language, or when you want a quick avatar update without rerecording. I treat it as a finishing tool, not a starter.

Q: Can I use this for podcast audio instead of video?
A: Yes, but you lose the visual clips. Most of the audio-to-text steps still apply. I'd recommend filming the podcast even if you publish audio-only, because the video pieces give you the most reuse.

Q: Which tool comes first if I'm starting from zero?
A: Claude. The writing layer carries the most weight in every other step. Set up the brand voice once and the rest of the stack gets faster.

# Claude Projects: Setting Up Your First One (Step by Step for Business Owners)

URL: https://kristamashore.ai/articles/claude-projects-setting-up-first-one
Pillar: Claude for Dummies: The AI Tools That Actually Matter
Published: 2026-05-24T16:04:35.664Z
Author: Krista Mashore

You've been chatting with Claude for months and re-explaining your business every time. Here's how to set up your first Claude Project so Claude already knows who you are.

You've been chatting with Claude for a couple of months. You like it, you use it for emails and the occasional rewrite, and then every single time you open a new chat you have to explain who you are, what your business does, who you sell to, and what your voice sounds like all over again. And then halfway through the conversation Claude forgets and starts writing like a HubSpot intern. I know. I did the same thing for almost a full year before I figured out what a Claude Project actually is, and once I did my whole AI life changed. So I want to walk you through setting up your first one. Not the influencer version with 47 screenshots and a paid template. The version a normal business owner can do in about 90 minutes one Saturday morning. If you want the step by step version of that, read Claude Skills: Build Your Brand Voice Skill Once and Reuse Forever . What a Claude Project actually is (in plain English) A Project is a dedicated workspace inside Claude where you upload reference files once, write a set of standing instructions once, and then every conversation you start inside that workspace already knows who you are. Think of it like hiring a new assistant and giving them a binder on day one instead of explaining the business from scratch every Monday. Three things make a Project different from a regular chat: You upload files that Claude can reference across every conversation inside that Project. You write custom instructions that load at the start of every conversation. And the conversations you have inside the Project stay grouped together, so you can come back to that one rewrite you did three weeks ago without scrolling through 400 random chats. That last part sounds boring and it's actually the thing that saves the most time once you get used to it. Why Projects beat just chatting When you chat with Claude in a fresh window, you're talking to a brilliant generalist who knows nothing about you. You spend the first ten messages getting Claude up to speed on your business, your tone, and what you actually want, and by the time the answer starts coming back, you're already tired. We go deeper on this in Brand Voice Fingerprinting: How to Capture How You Write So Claude Sounds Like You . A Project skips that whole opening act. You walk in, Claude already has your brand brain, your ideal client doc, and your voice rules loaded, and you start with the actual work. I'd estimate a good Project saves me 15 to 20 minutes per session because I'm not re-explaining anything. Across a week that's hours. The other thing nobody mentions: Claude tends to write better when it has context. Not slightly better. A lot better. A Claude with no context will hedge, generalize, and use the corporate words you hate. A Claude with your brand brain loaded sounds closer to you, because it has examples to pattern-match against. The 3 files to upload first Don't try to load 50 documents on day one. Pick three, get them right, and add more later as you find gaps. File 1: The Brand Brain This is one document, ideally 4 to 8 pages, that captures the spine of your business. Who you are, who you serve, what you sell, what you charge, your top three offers, your most common objections, your origin story in 3 paragraphs, and the words you use for the things in your world. If you call your audience "agents and lenders" don't let Claude default to "real estate professionals." That's what the brand brain is for. That is the same question behind The Authority Agent Operating System: The 5 Layers Every Service Business Needs in 2026 , which walks through it in detail. Build this in Google Docs first. Save it as a PDF. Upload it. File 2: The Ideal Client Doc A separate document because it gets edited more often. Who is the person you want to attract. Their pain points in their own words, not yours. The phrases they use when they describe their problem to a friend at dinner. The objections they have before they buy. The transformation they want. The transformation they actually need (sometimes different). What they've tried before and why it didn't work. I keep mine to 3 pages. Anything longer and Claude starts averaging across too many archetypes. File 3: The Voice Rules This is the file most people skip and it's the one that does the heaviest lifting. A voice rules doc lists the words you will never use, the words you do use, the sentence patterns you avoid, the formatting tics you have, and 4 to 6 paragraphs of writing you've personally written that you're happy with. Claude uses those samples to triangulate your voice. Without them, you get the default Claude voice with a polite hat on. If you want to skip ahead, I've got a full piece coming on building a brand voice Skill, which is the next step after a voice rules file. Same idea, more portable. The custom instructions to write Inside the Project you'll see a field for custom instructions. This is where most people leave it blank. Don't. Write something like this in plain English: "You are working inside the [Your Business] Project. Your job is to help me write, plan, and think out loud about my business. Always reference the brand brain, ideal client doc, and voice rules when generating any client-facing copy. Match my voice, not yours. When in doubt, ask before generating. Use contractions, vary sentence lengths, and no em-dashes. If you're about to use a corporate word like 'use' or 'use,' rewrite it before showing me. Default to specific examples and named clients, not generic advice." Adjust to taste. The whole instruction block should be maybe 200 to 400 words. Long enough to be useful, short enough that Claude can actually hold it all in working context. The "this is for my business" scaffold Once the files are in and the instructions are written, start your first conversation with what I call the scaffold prompt. Something like, "Read the brand brain and the ideal client doc. Summarize back to me in 5 bullets who this business is, who it serves, and what kind of voice I want. I want to confirm you've understood before I ask you to write anything." Claude will summarize. You'll find things that are wrong or weak. Fix the source docs, re-upload, summarize again. Two rounds of this and your Project is calibrated. I cannot stress this enough: spending an extra 20 minutes on calibration day saves you weeks of fixing bad output later. Pattern interrupt. The number one mistake I see people make at this stage is going straight from setup into "write me 10 LinkedIn posts." Don't. Have one conversation about your business with Claude where you don't ask for output. Just talk. See if the responses sound like someone who knows you. If yes, you're calibrated. If no, the docs need work. What to do once the first Project is humming You're going to want to make more. Resist for two weeks. Use this one Project for everything, and watch where it breaks. Maybe it's bad at writing emails specifically, maybe it loses voice on long-form, maybe it doesn't know your podcast guests. Those gaps tell you what your second Project should be (for me it was a content Project separate from a sales Project), and what additional files to add to your knowledge base. If you want the bigger system this Project sits inside, including the Skills layer that makes your voice portable across every Project, that's what I teach inside Level Up . Same setup we use internally on my team, end to end, no fluff.

## FAQ

Q: Do I need Claude Pro or higher to use Projects?
A: Projects are available on Claude's paid plans. Plan names and pricing change, so verify current pricing on Anthropic's site before subscribing. As a general rule, if you're using Claude for business you want a paid plan anyway because the free tier caps message volume.

Q: How many files can I upload to a single Project?
A: There's a per-Project knowledge limit and it's been raised more than once. Rather than quote a number that may be outdated, upload your three core files first, see how Claude handles them, then add more as needed. Most business owners do not need 50 files, they need 5 good ones.

Q: Are my uploaded files private?
A: Anthropic states that, by default, your inputs are not used to train their models on consumer plans. Policies change. If this matters for your business, read Anthropic's current data usage policy directly before uploading anything sensitive.

Q: Should I use a separate Project for each client?
A: For most solopreneurs, no. One Project for your business is enough. Agencies and coaches with multiple distinct client brands sometimes set up one Project per client. Start with one and split only when you feel friction.

Q: What if my voice changes over time?
A: Your Project is a living thing. Update your voice rules document every 60 to 90 days, re-upload the new version, and your Project evolves with you.

Q: Can I share a Project with my team?
A: Team plans support shared Projects. Personal plans have been more limited on sharing. Verify on Anthropic's current plan comparison if this matters to you.

# How to Build Your First AI Agent in n8n With No Coding (Real Walkthrough)

URL: https://kristamashore.ai/articles/build-ai-agent-n8n-no-coding
Pillar: The AI-Run Business
Published: 2026-05-24T16:04:35.664Z
Author: Krista Mashore

You don't need to code. You need an afternoon. Here's exactly how to build a lead-intake AI agent in n8n that qualifies submissions and books calls while you sleep.

You don't need to learn Python. You don't need a developer on retainer. You need a free afternoon, a Claude API key, and the willingness to drag boxes around on a canvas. That's it. I'm writing this for the business owner who keeps hearing "AI agents" and feels behind. You're not behind. You're 47 minutes away from owning your first one. Before you decide, it helps to read The Authority Agent Operating System: The 5 Layers Every Service Business Needs in 2026 . The agent we're building today: a lead-intake agent. Someone fills out a form on your site. The agent reads the submission, looks up the person on LinkedIn (or wherever), decides if they're qualified, drafts a personalized reply, and books a call on your calendar if they pass. All while you're at lunch. Why n8n and not some "no-code AI platform" There are a hundred tools promising magical AI agents in 5 minutes. Most of them are wrappers around OpenAI with a pretty UI and a $97/month subscription. n8n is different. It's an open-source workflow tool with a real AI agent node, and you can run it on a $5/month server or use their cloud version if you want zero infrastructure headaches. I like n8n because when something breaks at 11pm on a Tuesday, I can see exactly which step failed and fix it. The drag-drop tools that hide everything? Good luck debugging those. If you want the step by step version of that, read MCP Servers Explained: The 5 to Set Up First (For Non-Technical Business Owners) . Two paths to start: - n8n Cloud. Sign up at n8n.io, get a hosted instance in about 90 seconds. There's a free trial and paid tiers above that. Check their pricing page for current numbers, it shifts. - Self-hosted. Docker container on a $6/month Hetzner box, or one click on Railway. If you have a technical friend, ask them. If not, start with cloud. You can always migrate later. Don't let infrastructure paralysis stop you from building the actual thing. The 6 pieces of your lead-intake agent Here's the workflow we're building. Every box on the canvas is a node. You connect them with lines. That's the whole "coding." Webhook node … receives the form submission Set node … cleans up the data (name, email, phone, message) AI Agent node … this is where Claude does the thinking Cal.com or Calendly node … books the meeting Gmail node … sends a personalized reply Notion or Airtable node … logs everything for later That's the spine. You can add fancier stuff later (Slack notifications, CRM updates, lead scoring). Start with the spine. Step 1: The webhook In n8n, click the orange "+" to add a node. Search "Webhook." Drop it on the canvas. n8n gives you a unique URL. Take that URL and paste it into the form tool you use. Tally, Typeform, Jotform, even a basic HTML form on your site… all of them can POST to a webhook. Now when someone submits, n8n catches it instantly. (Quick aside, the first time I saw a webhook fire in real time, I felt like a wizard. It's the closest non-developers get to feeling like they wrote actual software.) Step 2: Clean the data with a Set node The webhook gives you raw form data. Usually messy. Names with weird capitalization, phone numbers in 8 different formats, emails with trailing spaces. The Set node lets you map fields to clean names. So `fields.email` becomes `email`. `fields.full_name` becomes `name`. You don't write code. You click dropdowns and pick the field you want. We go deeper on this in The AI-Run Business Stack Krista Uses Today (Full 2026 Breakdown) . Takes about 4 minutes. Step 3: The AI Agent node, where the magic happens This is the node that's going to do the actual thinking. Drag in the "AI Agent" node (n8n's Advanced AI section). You'll plug three things into it: - A model. Pick Claude (Anthropic) or OpenAI. I prefer Claude Sonnet for this kind of task because the responses sound more like a person and less like a chatbot. You'll need an API key from console.anthropic.com or platform.openai.com. - A system prompt. This is where you tell the agent who it is and what to do. - Tools (optional). The agent can call other nodes mid-thought. Cool, but skip this for v1. My system prompt looks roughly like this: You are the lead-intake assistant for [Your Business Name]. You receive form submissions from people interested in working with us. Your job is to: 1. Read the submission and decide if they look like a real prospect (ignore obvious spam, students doing research, agencies trying to sell us SEO). 2. If real, write a 4-sentence personalized reply that references something specific from their submission. 3. Output a JSON object with: qualified (boolean), reply_text (string), suggested_call_length (15 or 30). Tone: warm, direct, no corporate fluff. Sound like a real person who's read what they wrote. That's it. Save it. Test it with a fake submission. You'll see the agent's response in the right panel. Step 4: Calendar booking Add a Cal.com node. (Calendly works too, the n8n Calendly node has limited write actions last I checked, so Cal.com tends to be smoother for booking.) Configure it with your API key. Tell it to create a hold or send a booking link based on the `suggested_call_length` the agent returned. If your agent returns `qualified: false`, skip this step. Use an IF node to branch. Step 5: Send the reply Gmail node. Connect your account via OAuth (one click). Tell it to send `reply_text` from the AI agent to the email from the form. Set the from address, the subject, done. Pro tip: cc yourself on the first 20 emails the agent sends. Watch what it writes. Tweak the system prompt until you'd hit send yourself without editing. Step 6: Log it Airtable or Notion node. Append a row with the submission, the agent's decision, the timestamp. This is your audit trail. When the agent screws up (and it will, occasionally), you'll want this. What it actually costs to run Honest math, monthly: - n8n Cloud starter tier or a $6 self-host server - Anthropic API: pennies per submission on Claude Haiku, a few cents on Sonnet. For a business getting under 500 leads/month, you'll spend under $20. - Cal.com or Calendly: whatever you already pay - Gmail: free if you have Google Workspace So under $50/month for an agent that handles intake while you sleep. Compare that to a VA at $1,200/month who only works business hours and needs training. Three things that will go wrong (and they're fine) The first 5 emails will be slightly off. Tweak the prompt. Each tweak takes 60 seconds. You'll have a junk submission slip through as "qualified." Add a rule in the prompt: "If the message is shorter than 12 words OR doesn't mention what they need help with, mark qualified=false." The agent will book a call for someone who clearly didn't want one yet. Add a step: agent has to explicitly include `wants_call: true` before Cal.com runs. You iterate. You're building a system, not casting a spell. You don't need permission to start The agents you'll build next year start with the one you build this weekend. Stop saving the n8n tutorial for later. Open n8n.io, hit start free, and build the spine I just described. If you want the full version of this system, including the prompt templates I use across 6 agents in my own business, plus the qualification scoring rubric, that's all inside Level Up. Krista walks you through it on real screens, not theory. Get the AI System Inside Level Up →

## FAQ

Q: Do I need to know any code at all?
A: No. You connect nodes by dragging lines. You write English in the AI agent's system prompt. The only code-ish thing is referencing variables like {{$json.email}}, and n8n autocompletes those for you.

Q: Claude or OpenAI, which one?
A: For writing-heavy tasks like replies, summaries, and qualification decisions, Claude tends to sound more like a person. For most other tasks both work fine. Pick one and ship. You can swap models later without rebuilding the workflow.

Q: What if I get more than 500 leads a month?
A: Then you should pay attention to API costs and probably run n8n self-hosted. The cost still rarely breaks $100/month for most businesses at that volume.

Q: Can the agent actually book on my calendar without me approving?
A: Yes. If that feels too risky for week one, set Cal.com to create a hold that you confirm once you approve. After watching it work for a month, you can let it run free.

Q: What if the agent makes a bad decision?
A: Log every run. Review the logs weekly for the first month and adjust your system prompt. After 30 days the agent will outperform a junior VA on this task in most cases.

Q: How long until I have it running?
A: First time, give yourself 3 to 4 hours including setup. The second agent you build takes under an hour. By the fifth, you can do it on a Saturday morning.

# The Authority Agent Operating System: The 5 Layers Every Service Business Needs in 2026

URL: https://kristamashore.ai/articles/authority-agent-operating-system-5-layers
Pillar: The Authority Agent Operating System™
Published: 2026-05-24T16:04:35.664Z
Author: Krista Mashore

Most entrepreneurs build their AI stack backwards. Here are the five layers, in order, that make an AI system sound like you and run your business.

You bought another AI course this weekend, didn't you. Maybe two. I'm not judging, I've done the same thing more times than I want to admit, and the reason none of them stuck is not that you're lazy or that the tools are bad. It's that you skipped the part nobody talks about, which is the part where you decide what kind of business the AI is supposed to be running before you turn the AI on. Most entrepreneurs build the wrong thing first. They go straight to prompts and ChatGPT hacks before they've defined what their business even sounds like, and then they wonder why their LinkedIn posts read like a slightly drunk MBA student wrote them. So I want to give you the frame I use with my own team and with the coaching clients I work with, and it's the same frame I built my business on. I call it the Authority Agent Operating System, or AAOS, and it has five layers. The reason I'm writing this today is because I got off a call this morning with a coach who has spent eighteen thousand dollars on AI consultants in the last year and her content still sounds nothing like her. So. That is the same question behind Claude Projects: Setting Up Your First One (Step by Step for Business Owners) , which walks through it in detail. Layer 1: Brand Voice This is the foundation and it's the one almost everyone gets wrong. Brand voice is not a list of adjectives like "warm, professional, approachable." That is a Pinterest mood board, not a brand voice. A real brand voice is a documented, reusable artifact that captures how you write. The cadence. The words you use. The words you'd never use. The way you start sentences. The way you contradict yourself mid-paragraph because you thought of something better. If your AI doesn't have this layer, every other layer is contaminated. You can have the smartest agent in the world and it'll still sound like LinkedIn slop. The good news is Claude Skills, which Anthropic rolled out in 2025, make this layer portable. You write your voice into a Skill once and every project you start with Claude can call it. I'll do a whole separate piece on the exact fingerprinting process. For now, know this is layer one for a reason. Layer 2: Knowledge Your brain is layer two. Specifically the parts of your brain that don't live anywhere else yet. Your frameworks, your stories, your client case studies, the way you explain things on calls that nobody has ever transcribed. The pricing logic you carry around in your head. The seven objections you handle every week. For a closer look at this part, see Brand Voice Fingerprinting: How to Capture How You Write So Claude Sounds Like You . This is where Claude Projects come in. As of mid-2026, a Claude Project lets you upload a knowledge base of documents and set persistent custom instructions, so every conversation inside that project starts with your full context loaded. I have around 40 documents in my main Project, which is mostly transcripts from coaching calls, my book material, and the frameworks I use most. Why this matters: AI without your knowledge is an articulate stranger. AI with your knowledge is a junior version of you. And that's what we're building toward. Layer 3: Workflows Here's where most people start, which is why most people never finish. Workflows are the repeatable jobs the business does over and over. Content production. Lead follow-up. Onboarding emails. Proposal drafting. Refund handling. The dozens of small loops your business runs every week. Before AI can touch a workflow, you need to write it down. As in, describe it as steps a 19-year-old VA could follow. If you can't write the workflow down, AI cannot run it. Period. (I keep meeting people who want me to "AI-ify" a process they've never even documented. Sigh.) There is a fuller breakdown of this in The AI-Run Business Stack Krista Uses Today (Full 2026 Breakdown) . Tools I use here: n8n for the multi-step automations that string different apps together, and Make for the simpler ones. Both work fine. Pick the one that makes you less anxious when you look at the canvas. Layer 4: Agents This is the layer that's having a moment, and for good reason. An agent is not a single prompt. An agent is a small, focused worker that can make decisions and call tools on its own. The content-repurposing agent. The "did this lead respond" agent. The "draft three replies to these inbox messages in my voice" agent. The thing that changed agents in the last year and a half is the Model Context Protocol, or MCP. Without going too deep, MCP is the open standard that lets AI applications talk to your other tools. Your calendar. Your CRM. Your Notion. Your Drive. Before MCP, every connection was a custom build. Now it's closer to plug-and-play, and the stack has gotten big. For most service businesses, you don't need a swarm of agents. You need three or four good ones that handle the loops you do most often. Quality over quantity, always. Layer 5: Distribution The last layer, and the one I think is most underrated. Distribution is how the content, the conversations, and the offers leave your computer and reach a human. Where it goes. How often. In what format. I see entrepreneurs build beautiful AI content engines that produce thirty pieces of content a week and then post none of them because the publishing piece was never built. Don't do that. Build the pipe before you turn on the faucet. This is where you wire up your scheduler, your email platform, your podcast distribution, your YouTube uploader. n8n handles a lot of this for me. You'll figure out your own stack. Why most entrepreneurs build this backwards They start with layer four. The shiny agent. The autonomous AI worker. And then they wonder why it sounds wrong, knows nothing, has nowhere to go, and operates on workflows that were never documented. It's like buying a Ferrari before you have a driveway, gas, or a destination. You've got a thing that looks expensive sitting in your front yard doing nothing. Build in order: voice, knowledge, workflows, agents, distribution. Each layer assumes the one below it. Skip a layer and the whole thing wobbles. I built my own AAOS over about fourteen months, and yes that's longer than most YouTube videos make it sound. The voice layer took me almost two months on its own because I kept tweaking the Skill. The agents came last and they came fast, because the foundation was already there. What to do this week Don't try to build all five layers at once. Pick layer one. Spend a Saturday with a coffee and a notepad, pull out twenty pieces of your past content (emails, social posts, voice memos), and start cataloguing what makes your writing sound like you. That's your starting point. If you want the full step-by-step on how I built mine, including the exact prompts, the Skill structure, and the agent setups, I walk through the whole thing inside my Level Up training. It's the same system I use to run a business that produces more content than most marketing teams with a fraction of the headcount. Come grab it at kristamashore.com/LevelUp .

## FAQ

Q: Do I need to be technical to build the Authority Agent Operating System?
A: No. The hard part is not the tech, it's the thinking. If you can write down how you do your work, you can build this. Tools like Claude Projects and n8n have gotten friendly enough that no-code people use them every day.

Q: How long does this take to set up?
A: Plan on a quarter, not a weekend. The brand voice layer alone takes a few focused sessions. Workflows take longer because you have to document things you've been doing on autopilot.

Q: What if I already use ChatGPT, not Claude?
A: The five layers still apply. Brand voice, knowledge, workflows, agents, distribution. The tools change, the architecture doesn't. I personally use Claude because the voice layer holds up better for long-form writing, but pick what works for you.

Q: Which layer do I do first if I'm starting from scratch?
A: Layer one, brand voice. Always. Without it, everything downstream sounds wrong.

Q: Can I outsource this build?
A: You can outsource layers three through five. You cannot outsource layer one and layer two, because that's your brain and your voice. Those have to come from you, even if someone else types them up.

Q: How much should I expect to spend on tools?
A: For a solo or small-team business, under two hundred a month covers it for most people, with Claude, an automation tool like n8n or Make, and a scheduler. Costs scale up if you add a CRM integration or a custom agent stack.

# The AI-Run Business Stack Krista Uses Today (Full 2026 Breakdown)

URL: https://kristamashore.ai/articles/ai-run-business-stack-2026
Pillar: The AI-Run Business
Published: 2026-05-24T16:04:35.664Z
Author: Krista Mashore

Not a list of cool tools. The actual 6 AI products running my business this month, what they cost, and where each one is still rough.

I get this question every other week, on stage and in DMs. "Krista, what's actually in your stack? Like, what do you really use, not the sponsored stuff, the real one." Fair. Here it is. The actual tools running my business as of this month, what each one does, what it costs, and where each one is still rough. This isn't a list of every shiny tool I've tried. This is the surviving stack after I cut everything that didn't earn its keep. The principle behind the stack One rule: every tool has to either save me hours or earn me money. Not "be cool." Not "have AI features." Save time or make money. If it does neither after 60 days, it goes. The second rule. I'd rather have 6 tools I deeply use than 30 I half-use. Half-used tools are worse than no tool, because they put data in places I forget to look. This connects directly to How to Build Your First AI Agent in n8n With No Coding (Real Walkthrough) . The 6 core tools 1. Claude (writing and agents) , ~$20/month for Pro Claude is the brain. I use it for almost all of my long-form writing, content repurposing, sales page drafts, email replies that need actual thought, and increasingly as the model powering my AI agents (more on those below). Why Claude and not ChatGPT or Gemini. The writing voice. It's the only model I've used that doesn't make me rewrite every other sentence to sound like me. ChatGPT writes like a startup employee giving a TED talk. Gemini writes like a smart intern who reads a lot of HBR. Claude writes like a person who actually finished a draft. Cost: Claude Pro subscription is in the $20/month range for individual use last I checked. API usage for agents is separate and pay-as-you-go. We probably spend $80-150/month combined across team usage at this point, though that fluctuates. Where it's still rough. Long context windows are great, but when I dump 40,000 words of source material, it sometimes prioritizes the wrong parts. Solution: I summarize down to about 8,000 words before asking it to write. 2. n8n (workflow automation) , ~$20-50/month depending on tier n8n is my workflow brain. Anywhere I'd previously hire a VA to "do this every time that happens," n8n does it now. Lead intake. Follow-up sequences. Content distribution. Cross-posting from one platform to another. I'm running self-hosted (well, my team is, I'm not touching the server) but n8n Cloud is fine for most people. Their pricing page has the current tiers, I'd just check those rather than trust a number I wrote down 3 months ago. The practical side of this is covered in MCP Servers Explained: The 5 to Set Up First (For Non-Technical Business Owners) . Where it's still rough. The community nodes for newer platforms can be flaky. We've had 2 workflows break because a third-party node updated and changed the schema. Stick to the official nodes when possible, or build in error handling. 3. Fathom (meeting AI) , free tier or paid plans Every Zoom I'm on, Fathom is in there taking notes. It records, transcribes, summarizes, identifies action items, and lets me search across every call I've ever had. So when a client says "remember when you mentioned that thing about lead magnets 4 months ago," I find it in 8 seconds instead of guessing. The free tier covered me for a long time. We upgraded to paid because the team plan lets us share recordings across team members and includes a few features like CRM sync. I'd check their pricing page for what's current. Why Fathom and not Fireflies or Otter? Honestly, all three work. I picked Fathom because the summaries were the cleanest of the three when I tested. Fireflies is fine. Otter is the OG and has its fans. Where it's still rough. Like all meeting AI, it occasionally hears something wrong and the summary inherits the error. I scan every summary before I trust it. Takes 30 seconds, worth it. Before you decide, it helps to read The 7 AI Tools Running Krista's Content Engine Right Now . 4. Sales follow-up AI (Lindy or similar) , pricing varies I'm being deliberately vague here because I'm still actively testing this category. Lindy is one of the platforms I've evaluated for AI agents that handle inbound sales conversations, follow-ups, scheduling. There are several competitors emerging. What I want this category to do: pick up after my team's first reply, follow up on a cadence, qualify the lead, book the call. Stop the "lead goes cold because nobody followed up on day 7" problem. Where it's still rough. Honestly? This whole category is the roughest part of my stack. The platforms can sound robotic if you don't tune them carefully. I've also seen one tool send a follow-up to a lead AFTER they'd already booked, which is the kind of thing that erodes trust. So I'm hedging. I'm not telling you "go buy Lindy today." I'm telling you this is a category to watch and to pilot carefully. If you want my candid take when you're in Level Up, I'll tell you exactly where each platform stands in my testing. The category is moving fast enough that I'd rather give you in-the-moment intel than something I wrote down 6 weeks ago that's already outdated. 5. Notion (SOPs and operations brain) , ~$8-15/month per user on team plan Notion is where the business lives. Every SOP, every process, every project, every client note, every offer template. If a process exists, it lives in Notion. If it lives nowhere else, it doesn't exist. The reason I keep Notion specifically (and not ClickUp, Asana, Monday, or any of the others) is that Notion plays unusually well with AI. They've put real effort into MCP integration. So my AI agents can read and write Notion pages, which means my operations brain is also my agents' brain. That matters more every month. Where it's still rough. Notion's search is okay, not great. Their built-in AI is fine for inline tasks but I still prefer dropping content into Claude for serious thinking. 6. Gmail with MCP triage , Workspace pricing, plus AI usage This isn't a separate product, it's a setup. Gmail (via Google Workspace) connected through an MCP server so my AI agents can read my inbox, draft replies, label, search, and triage. The result: my morning inbox review went from 45 minutes to about 12. The AI does the first pass. I confirm or edit. Google Workspace pricing is a few dollars per user per month for the lower tiers, last I checked. The MCP server is free open-source, you just need to be willing to set it up (see my separate article on MCP servers if you haven't). Where it's still rough. Permissions and OAuth scopes. Granting an AI agent write access to your inbox is the kind of thing that should make you slightly nervous. I started with read-only for 3 weeks, then graduated to draft-only, then graduated to "can send if marked auto-send" with a human review queue for anything else. The total monthly cost, honestly Adding it up rough monthly numbers for a small team: - Claude: $20-200 depending on whether you're on Pro or paying for API agents - n8n: $20-50 if cloud, less if self-hosted - Fathom: $0-50 - Sales follow-up AI: $50-200 (testing category) - Notion: $30-90 for a small team - Google Workspace: $30-100 for a small team So somewhere between $150 and $700/month total for a small operation, depending on team size and how much you push usage. Compared to one mid-level operations hire at $5,000-8,000/month, the stack is a steal. What I cut A short list of things I tested in the last 12 months and removed: - 3 different "all-in-one" AI marketing platforms. Every one of them did 5 things mediocrely instead of one thing well. - 2 separate CRMs trying to replace what Notion already does for me. - One "agent builder" that promised the moon and shipped a thin wrapper around OpenAI. This isn't shade. It's that my business doesn't need everything that exists. It needs the 6 tools above doing their jobs. The stack will change. The principles won't. By 2027, half this list might look different. New tools will replace some, mergers will eat others. What won't change: I run my business on tools where the AI can see my data and act on it, not tools where I copy-paste forever between siloed apps.
